well-relationships.title: Relationships & respect: friends, consent, love and identity
well-relationships.description: Friendships, peer pressure, consent at every age, healthy and unhealthy relationships, gender and identity, POSH at work and talking to children — respectful, inclusive and practical.

courses.title: Friendships, peer pressure, conflict & crushes
courses.summary: What makes a friendship healthy, handling peer pressure, resolving conflicts without wrecking friendships, and the confusing world of crushes, rejection and respect.
outcomes: Learners can describe qualities of healthy friendships
Learners can resist negative peer pressure with scripts
Learners can resolve conflicts using a step-by-step method
Learners can handle crushes and rejection respectfully
courses.guardianNote: Friendships, peer pressure, conflict resolution, crushes and handling rejection for ages 10–15. Age-appropriate, non-explicit, focused on kindness, communication and self-respect.

scenes.text: Mira joins mid-year. A popular group invites her — but only if she stops sitting with quiet Sana.
Mira notices the group mocks others often.
She keeps Sana as a friend and slowly makes others who are kind. 'Friends should make you feel more like yourself, not less.'

steps.title: Healthy friendship signs
steps.body: Mutual respect · trust · you can be yourself · disagreements are talked through · they're happy for your success · they respect your 'no' · effort goes both ways · you feel safe and mostly good around them.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body: Frequent put-downs disguised as jokes · making you choose between them and others · spreading your secrets · pressuring you into things · only around when they need something · you feel anxious or drained most of the time.

steps.title: Solved example: friendship check
steps.body:
Score each 0–2: respect, trust, fun, support, honesty.
Friend A: 2,2,2,1,2 = 9/10 → strong.
Friend B: 0,1,2,0,0 = 3/10 → many warning signs; talk to them, or spend more time with others.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking more friends = better; a few good friends matter more.
- Staying in a friendship that hurts out of fear of being alone.
- Expecting friends to read your mind.

items.text: Happy when you win a prize
Makes you choose between them and others
Mocks you in front of others 'as a joke'
Only calls when they need homework

quiz.why: A healthy friend respects your 'no' and your choices. Forcing, mocking or making you choose are signs of an unhealthy friendship.
Regular put-downs disguised as jokes hurt you and are a warning sign of an unhealthy friendship. Real banter is fun for both people.
Quality matters more than quantity, because a few friends who respect and support you are better than many who don't.

quiz.q: Feeling drained around a friend often…
quiz.why: Often feeling drained around a friend is worth noticing, as it may mean the friendship is unhealthy for you. It does not mean you are weak.
Friends cannot read your mind, so communicate what you feel and need. Expecting them to guess leads to misunderstandings.

lessons.title: Peer pressure: saying no and staying friends

scenes.text: Friends plan to bunk the last period and go to the mall. 'Don't be a baby, come!'
Rishi doesn't want to.
'Nah, I've got a test. See you tomorrow.' Nobody really cares, and he isn't left out the next day.

steps.title: Types of peer pressure
steps.body:
- **Positive**: friends encourage you to study, try sport, be kind.
- **Negative**: pressure to bunk, cheat, smoke/vape, drink, bully, share photos, take risks.
- **Spoken** (direct dares) or **unspoken** (everyone's doing it, so you feel you must).

steps.title: Refusal scripts
steps.body:
- 'No thanks.' (Repeat if needed — the 'broken record'.)
- 'Not my thing.'
- 'My parents would ground me for life.'
- 'I've got practice.'
- Suggest something else: 'Let's play cricket instead.'
- Leave and text a code word to a parent.

steps.title: Solved example: think ahead (if–then plans)
steps.body:
'**If** someone offers me a vape at the party, **then** I'll say "No thanks" and go to the snack table.'
'**If** they dare me to bunk, **then** I'll say I've got a test.'
If–then plans make it easier to act under pressure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing 'everyone' is doing it — surveys usually show fewer people do risky things than teens assume.
- Over-explaining your no.
- Feeling you'll lose all friends — real friends stay.

a.text: A friend with an older brother's bike says, 'Hop on, no helmet needed, it's just 5 minutes.'

choices.label: 'No helmet, no ride. I'll walk and meet you there.'
Get on so you don't look scared

b.text: He starts speeding. You feel unsafe.

choices.label: 'Stop here, I'm getting off,' then walk and tell an adult

end1.text: You arrive safely. Nobody remembers it by evening.

end2.text: You're safe. Next time you'll say no at the start.

quiz.why: Positive peer pressure pushes you toward good choices, like friends encouraging you to study. Cheating, bunking and vaping are negative pressure.
In the broken-record technique you calmly repeat 'No thanks' as often as needed. You don't need to argue, agree or explain more.
If–then plans prepare your response ahead of time, so you can act under pressure instead of freezing. Example: 'If offered a vape, then I say no and walk away.'
'Everyone is doing it' is usually an overestimate, because risky behaviour looks more common than it is. It is not a fact or a law.
Real friends accept your 'no' and don't force you. Those who laugh, pressure or drop you for refusing are not acting as friends.

lessons.title: Resolving conflict without losing the friendship

scenes.text: Riya feels she did all the work on the project; Aditya thinks she took over.
They stop talking for a week.
Their teacher guides them through 'I-statements' and listening. They split the next project fairly.

steps.title: Five-step conflict method
steps.body:
1. **Cool down** first (breathe, walk).
2. **Each person speaks** using I-statements: 'I felt ___ when ___.'
3. **Listen and reflect**: 'So you felt ___ because ___?'
4. **Brainstorm solutions** together.
5. **Agree and check back** later.

steps.title: Solved example: rewrite blame into I-statements
steps.body:
Blame: 'You always take over!' → I: 'I felt left out when the slides were finished without me.'
Blame: 'You never do anything!' → I: 'I felt stressed when I was doing most of the research.'

steps.title: Apologising and forgiving
steps.body: A real apology names the action, takes responsibility and offers repair. Forgiving doesn't mean forgetting or allowing it again — it means letting go of revenge. Some friendships end, and that's OK too.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Fighting over chat (tone gets lost) — talk in person or call.
- Dragging others into 'sides'.
- Bringing up every old issue at once.

quiz.why: The first step in a conflict is to cool down, as shouting or posting when angry makes things worse. Then talk when calm.
Reflecting means repeating back what you heard, so the other person feels understood and you check you got it right.

quiz.q: Best medium for a serious fight:
quiz.why: Serious fights are best handled in person or by call, where tone and intent are clear. Text, memes and public posts get misread and make it worse.
Forgiving means letting go of revenge and resentment. It doesn't mean forgetting everything or allowing the same behaviour again.
An I-statement says how you feel without blaming, like 'I felt left out when…'. 'You never' and 'You always' blame and start fights.

scenes.text: Kunal, 13, likes Tanya and writes her a note.
She says kindly, 'Thanks, but I just want to be friends.'
He's sad for a few days, talks to his elder cousin, and they stay friendly. 'Respecting her answer felt like the grown-up thing.'

steps.title: Crushes are normal
steps.body: Having a crush — on a classmate, a celebrity, someone of any gender — is a normal part of growing up. Some people have many crushes, some none; both are normal. You don't have to act on feelings, and there's no rush to date.

steps.title: If you share your feelings
steps.body: Do it privately, simply and respectfully — not through dares, public 'proposals' or group pressure. Accept any answer. **No means no** — repeated asking, following, or messaging after a no is harassment.

steps.title: Solved example: handling rejection
steps.body:
1. Feel it — sadness is normal.
2. Don't blame or insult the other person, or spread rumours.
3. Talk to a friend or trusted adult.
4. Do things you enjoy.
5. Remember: one person's answer isn't a verdict on your worth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Teasing classmates about crushes or pairing them up — can be humiliating.
- Thinking a 'no' is a challenge to win.
- Sharing someone's message or photo to mock them.

statements.s: Having a crush is a normal part of growing up.
If someone says no, asking again and again shows love.
Not having crushes is also normal.
Public 'proposals' can pressure the other person.

quiz.why: If someone says 'just friends', respect it. Asking again, getting angry or spreading rumours is disrespectful and can become harassment.
Crushes can be on anyone and are all normal at this age. They are not wrong or limited to classmates or celebrities.

options: talk to a friend, do things you enjoy
quiz.why: After rejection, talk to a friend and do things you enjoy, which helps you cope. Insulting, stalking or not eating hurts you or the other person.
Repeated messages after someone says no is harassment, because it ignores their choice and makes them uncomfortable. It is not romance or persistence.
Teasing classmates about crushes can humiliate them. It is not harmless or kind, even if you mean it as fun.

questions.why: A healthy friend respects your 'no'. Forcing you, mocking you or spreading your secrets are signs of a bad friendship.
Peer pressure can be positive, like encouraging study, or negative, like pushing risky acts. It is real and not only one kind.
Crushes are a normal part of growing up. They are not an illness, wrong or illegal.
A clear 'No thanks.' is a strong refusal. 'Maybe' or silence is unclear and leaves room for more pressure.
The first step in conflict is to cool down, because shouting, arguing or posting while angry makes it worse. Then talk calmly.
After a no, respect it. Asking again, sulking publicly or threatening ignores the other person's choice.

questions.q: Assertion: Fighting over chat often worsens conflict. Reason: Tone and intent get lost in text.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. In chat, tone and intent get lost, so words get misread and fights grow; talk in person or by call.

options: 'If offered a vape, then I'll say no and walk away'
questions.why: An if–then plan names a situation and your action, like 'If offered a vape, then I'll say no and walk away'. Plans like 'I'll decide then' or 'bunk' don't prepare you.
Making you choose between friends is a control behaviour and a warning sign. Listening, celebrating you and keeping secrets are healthy.

questions.q: Case: Friends dare Rahul to propose publicly to a girl. Best advice?
options: Don't — share feelings privately and respectfully, if at all
questions.why: A public proposal on a dare can embarrass and pressure the girl. Share feelings privately and respectfully, if at all, and don't record or turn it into a prank.
Add the scores: 1 + 0 + 2 + 0 + 1 = 4, so the total is 4/10.

questions.q: Turn 'You never help!' into an I-statement:
options: 'I feel stressed when I do most of the work.'
questions.why: An I-statement names your feeling and the situation without blaming: 'I feel stressed when I do most of the work.' 'You're lazy' or 'You always…' blame the person.

questions.q: Why do teens overestimate risky behaviour among peers?
options: Visible stories and bragging distort perceived norms
questions.why: Risky acts are talked about and bragged about more than quiet choices, so they seem more common than they are. Visible stories distort perceived norms.

options: Names the action, takes responsibility, offers repair
questions.why: A real apology names what you did, takes responsibility and offers to repair. 'Sorry you're upset', 'It was a joke' or 'You started it' avoid responsibility.

questions.q: Case: After rejection, Kunal wants to post her messages to mock her. Best guidance?
options: Don't — that's harassment; talk to someone and move on
questions.why: Posting someone's private messages to mock them is harassment and harms them. Talk to a trusted person and move on instead.

options: A friend pressures you to bunk
A friend dares you to shoplift
A friend invites you to join a coding club
questions.why: Positive influence is a friend inviting you to something constructive like a coding club. Pressure to bunk, shoplift or sharing your secret is negative.

questions.q: Case: A friend keeps 'joking' about your weight in front of others. Best first step?
options: Tell them privately with an I-statement and set a boundary
questions.why: Tell them privately with an I-statement and set a boundary, such as 'I feel hurt when you joke about my weight; please stop'. Laughing, insulting back or not eating doesn't solve it.

courses.title: Consent at every age: asking, listening and the law
courses.summary: Consent from everyday life to relationships: the FRIES model, how to ask and how to read 'no' (including non-verbal no), pressure, coercion and power, alcohol and consent, digital consent, and what Indian law says.
outcomes: Learners can define consent using FRIES
Learners can ask for consent and recognise verbal and non-verbal refusal
Learners can identify pressure and coercion
Learners can explain why intoxication prevents consent
Learners can state key Indian laws on age of consent and harassment
courses.guardianNote: Consent explained for teenagers: what it is, how to ask and read it, pressure and coercion, alcohol and consent, digital consent, and Indian law (age of consent 18 under POCSO). Non-explicit, values-based and practical.

scenes.text: Aman picks up Neha's phone to scroll her photos. 'Hey, ask first!' she says.
Their teacher uses it: 'Consent isn't only about bodies — it's about respecting people's choices.'
The class builds a consent checklist together.

steps.title: FRIES
steps.body:
Consent must be:
- **F**reely given — no pressure, threats or guilt.
- **R**eversible — you can change your mind anytime.
- **I**nformed — you know what you're agreeing to.
- **E**nthusiastic — a clear, happy yes, not a reluctant 'fine'.
- **S**pecific — yes to one thing isn't yes to everything.

steps.title: Consent in everyday life
steps.body: Hugging, borrowing things, sharing photos, reading messages, tagging someone, telling someone's secret, medical decisions (with parents for children). Practising it in small things builds respect for big ones.

steps.title: Solved example: is it consent?
steps.body:
(a) 'Can I hug you?' 'Yes!' → **yes** (free, enthusiastic, specific).
(b) 'Fine, whatever…' after repeated asking → **not freely given**.
(c) Agreed to a photo, not to it being posted → **specific**: posting needs a new yes.
(d) Said yes yesterday, says no today → **reversible**: it's no.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Silence or no response = yes (it doesn't).
- 'We're friends/dating, so it's always fine' — every time needs consent.
- Consent is a one-time contract — it's ongoing.

pairs: Yes to one thing isn't yes to all

quiz.why: Saying 'Fine, whatever' after pressure is not freely given consent. Consent must be a free choice, not something given just to end the pressure.

quiz.q: Yes to a photo, not posting:
quiz.why: Consent is specific: yes to a photo is not yes to posting it. Ask again for each new thing.
Silence is not a yes. Consent needs a clear sign of agreement, and no response is not agreement.
Consent can be withdrawn at any time. A person can change their mind even after saying yes.
Consent applies to everyday things like hugs, photos and borrowing items, and to relationships. It is not only for strangers or adults.

scenes.text: At a cousin's sangeet, Vikram keeps pulling Riya onto the dance floor.
She smiles awkwardly, pulls her hand back and looks away.
His sister says, 'She's saying no without words.' Vikram stops and apologises.

steps.title: How to ask
steps.body: Simple and pressure-free: 'Do you want to…?' 'Is this OK?' 'Would you like to, or not today?' — and be genuinely fine with either answer.

steps.title: No can look like…
steps.body: 'No', 'Not now', 'I'm not sure', 'Maybe later', changing the subject, silence, pulling away, stiff body, avoiding eye contact, nervous laughter, crying, freezing. **Anything less than a clear yes = stop and check.**

steps.title: Solved example: respond to an unclear signal
steps.body:
Situation: you ask a friend to go to a party; they hesitate.
- Step 1: Notice the hesitation.
- Step 2: Check: 'No pressure — want to skip it?'
- Step 3: Accept the answer without sulking or guilt-tripping.
That's how trust grows.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'They didn't say no' — only a clear yes counts.
- Asking again and again until they give in — that's pressure.
- Sulking or getting angry after a no.

activity.prompt: Clear yes, or stop and check?

items.text: Nervous laugh and changes the subject

quiz.q: Anything less than a clear yes means…
quiz.why: Anything less than a clear yes means stop and check. A maybe or hesitation is not agreement.
Pulling away is a non-verbal no. Consent can be shown or refused through body language, not only words.
Asking 'Is this OK?' gives the other person a real choice. 'You owe me' or 'Everyone does it' is pressure, and not asking skips consent.
After a no, accept it without sulking. Keeping on asking or guilt-tripping pressures them and ignores their choice.
Freezing is not consent. People may freeze from fear or shock, so only a clear freely-given yes counts.

scenes.text: Sameer's girlfriend keeps saying, 'If you loved me you would…' about things he isn't ready for.
He feels guilty for saying no.
A counsellor explains: guilt-tripping is pressure, and love respects limits.

steps.title: Coercion
steps.body: Getting a 'yes' through pressure, guilt ('if you loved me'), threats ('I'll leave/tell everyone'), repeated nagging, bribery, or using power (age, popularity, position, money) is **not consent**. Power imbalances — teacher/student, coach/player, boss/employee, adult/child — make free consent impossible or very difficult.

steps.title: Alcohol, drugs and consent
steps.body: A person who is drunk, high, asleep, unconscious or confused **cannot consent**. Drink-spiking is a crime. If someone is intoxicated, the right thing is to help them get home safely — not take advantage.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the pressure
steps.body:
Lines: (1) 'Everyone our age does it.' (2) 'You're so immature.' (3) 'I'll break up with you.' (4) 'Just this once.' (5) 'Okay, no worries, maybe another time.'
→ 1–4 are **pressure**; 5 is **respect**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'They agreed in the end, so it's fine' — not if they were pressured.
- 'They were drunk too, so it's equal' — intoxication removes capacity to consent.
- Believing gifts or money create an obligation — they don't.

statements.s: 'If you loved me you would' is a form of pressure.
An intoxicated person can give valid consent.
Gifts create an obligation to say yes.
Power differences make free consent harder.

quiz.q: 'I'll break up with you if you don't' is…
quiz.why: Threatening to break up unless someone agrees is coercion, because it pressures them. Consent must be given freely, without threats.
A sleeping person cannot consent, because they are unable to agree at that moment. An earlier yes or a relationship does not change this.
A coach and player is a power imbalance, because the coach has authority over the player. That can make it hard to say no freely.
'No worries, maybe another time' respects the no without pressure. 'Everyone does it', 'Just once' and insults pressure the person.
Drink-spiking is a crime. It takes away someone's ability to choose and is dangerous; it is never a prank.

lessons.title: Consent online and the law in India

scenes.text: Tanvi screenshots a friend's private chat and posts it 'for laughs'.
The friend is humiliated; the school calls both families.
Tanvi learns digital consent matters — and that some sharing is illegal.

steps.title: Digital consent
steps.body: Ask before: posting photos of others, tagging, sharing screenshots of private chats, adding people to groups, sharing location. Never pressure anyone to send photos or share passwords. **Reading someone's phone without permission breaks trust.**

steps.title: Indian law (topic level)
steps.body:
- **Age of consent is 18** (POCSO Act 2012): any sexual act with a person under 18 is an offence, regardless of 'agreement'.
- **Sexual harassment**, stalking (including online), voyeurism and sharing private images without consent are offences under the **BNS** and **IT Act**.
- Workplaces: **POSH Act 2013**. Child marriage is prohibited (**Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006**: 18 for women, 21 for men).
- Reporting: **112**, **1098** (under 18), **1930**/cybercrime.gov.in, women's helpline **181**.

steps.title: Solved example: digital consent check
steps.body:
Before posting a group photo:
1. Does everyone look OK with it? Ask.
2. Any location or school info visible?
3. Would anyone be embarrassed or put at risk?
4. If anyone says no → don't post, or crop/blur.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

items: Ask before posting or tagging others
Never share screenshots of private chats
Never pressure anyone for photos or passwords
Ask before adding someone to a group
Respect when someone wants a photo deleted

quiz.why: The age of consent in India is 18, and under POCSO anyone under 18 is a child who cannot legally consent to sexual acts.

quiz.q: Posting a private chat screenshot without consent…
quiz.why: Posting a private chat screenshot without consent breaks trust and can hurt the person. It is not funny or required.
The Women's Helpline number is 181. 1098 is Childline, 14416 is Tele-MANAS, and 1930 is for cyber fraud.

quiz.q: Legal marriage age for women in India:
quiz.why: Under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (PCMA), the legal minimum marriage age for women in India is 18 (21 for men in that law). So 18 is the answer here.
Online stalking is an offence under Indian law (BNS and IT laws). It is not harmless or romantic.

questions.why: In FRIES, R stands for Reversible: consent can be withdrawn at any time. The other letters are Freely given, Informed, Enthusiastic and Specific.
Silence is not a yes, because consent needs a clear agreement. Not saying no doesn't mean saying yes.
The age of consent in India is 18. Under that age, a person is a child under the law (POCSO).
Pulling away is a non-verbal no. Treat it as a refusal, not a game, joke or yes.
An intoxicated person cannot consent, because alcohol or drugs affect judgement and ability to decide. So any agreement is not valid.
The Women's Helpline number is 181. 1098 is Childline and 1930 is for cyber fraud.

questions.q: Assertion: Consent obtained by guilt-tripping is not valid. Reason: Consent must be freely given.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Consent has to be freely given, so a yes got through guilt-tripping is pressured and not valid.

options: yes to one thing isn't yes to everything
questions.why: Specific means yes to one thing is not yes to everything. Agreeing to one act doesn't cover others or future times.
'You owe me after the gift' is coercion because it uses a favour to pressure someone. 'Is this OK?', 'Want to?' and 'No worries' respect choice.

questions.q: Case: A friend agreed to a photo but asks you not to post it. You…
questions.why: Consent is specific: agreeing to a photo does not mean agreeing to its posting. If they ask you not to post, respect it and don't share it.
Enthusiastic consent is a clear, willing yes like 'Yes, I'd really like that!'. Silence, 'Fine' or 'I guess…' show hesitation, not real agreement.

questions.q: Why is free consent difficult with a large power imbalance?
options: Fear of consequences can force a 'yes'
questions.why: With a large power imbalance, the weaker person may fear consequences, so a 'yes' may be forced. This makes the consent not freely given.
The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006 prohibits child marriage in India. POSH deals with workplace harassment, the IT Act with cyber matters and COTPA with tobacco.

questions.q: Case: Someone said yes yesterday, no today. Correct?
questions.why: Consent can be withdrawn, so today's no stands over yesterday's yes. Asking until you get a yes is pressure.

questions.q: Case: At a party a friend is very drunk and someone wants to take them to a room. Best action?
options: Intervene, keep your friend with trusted people, get them home safely, alert an adult
questions.why: A very drunk person cannot consent, so step in: keep your friend with trusted people, get them home safely and alert an adult. Ignoring, joining or recording leaves them at risk.

questions.q: Which statement about consent and relationships is TRUE?
options: Being in a relationship never replaces the need for consent
questions.why: Being in a relationship never replaces the need for consent; it must be asked for and given every time. Dating, marriage or gifts don't mean a permanent yes.

questions.q: Case: A 17-year-old says their 'agreement' makes a sexual act with an adult legal. Correct?
options: No — under POCSO it's an offence because they're under 18
questions.why: Under POCSO, anyone under 18 cannot legally consent, so a sexual act with an adult is an offence even if the 17-year-old 'agrees'. Online or parental agreement doesn't change this.

courses.title: Healthy relationships, red flags & breakups
courses.summary: What a healthy relationship looks like, the spectrum from healthy to abusive, controlling and jealous behaviour, digital dating abuse, how to end a relationship safely and cope with breakups, and where to get help.
outcomes: Learners can describe the features of healthy relationships
Learners can recognise red flags including control and digital abuse
Learners can explain the cycle of abuse and why leaving is hard
Learners can plan a safe breakup and cope afterwards
Learners can name support services
courses.guardianNote: For ages 15–19: healthy vs unhealthy relationships, controlling behaviour and digital dating abuse, breakups, and how to get help. Non-explicit, focused on respect, equality and safety (112, 181, 1098, 14416).

scenes.text: In college, Rhea's partner encourages her to join the debate team and is proud when she wins.
Her friend Kavya's partner checks her phone daily and sulks when she meets friends.
Rhea realises: love should make your world bigger, not smaller.

steps.title: Healthy relationship features
steps.body: Respect · trust · honesty · equality (decisions shared) · good communication · independence (own friends, hobbies, goals) · support · safety · consent always · disagreements handled without fear.

steps.title: The spectrum
steps.body: **Healthy** (respect, equality) → **Unhealthy** (poor communication, jealousy, some control, disrespect) → **Abusive** (fear, control, threats, violence, sexual coercion, isolation). Relationships can move along the spectrum — notice changes early.

steps.title: Solved example: the relationship check
steps.body:
Rate 0–2: Do I feel safe? Can I see my friends? Do we decide things together? Is my 'no' respected? Am I free to keep my phone private?
Score 9–10 healthy · 5–8 some concerns — talk, set boundaries · 0–4 or any fear → seek help.

steps.title: Common myths
steps.body:
- 'Jealousy shows love' — possessiveness is control.
- 'Fighting is passion' — constant fights and fear aren't healthy.
- 'They'll change after marriage' — patterns usually continue.

items.text: Threatens to hurt you if you leave
Pressures you sexually after you said no

quiz.why: A healthy relationship is built on equality and respect. Fear, control and isolation are signs of an unhealthy one.
Calling jealousy 'love' is a myth. Possessiveness is about control, while real care trusts and respects the other person.
Feeling afraid in a relationship is never normal or romantic, so seek help from a trusted adult or helpline. Ignoring it can let harm continue.

options: keeping your own friends and goals
quiz.why: Independence means keeping your own friends and goals while in a relationship. Healthy partners support this rather than demand all your time.
Unhealthy patterns such as control, jealousy or disrespect usually continue after marriage, and often get worse. Marriage doesn't fix them, so notice red flags early.

lessons.title: Red flags: control and digital dating abuse

scenes.text: Arjun's girlfriend insists he share live location 24×7 'so she knows he's safe'.
She gets angry if he doesn't reply in 5 minutes and asks for his passwords.
His friend points out these are control red flags, not care.

steps.title: Control red flags
steps.body: Extreme jealousy · checking phone/messages · demanding passwords or live location · deciding what you wear or who you meet · isolating you from friends/family · constant put-downs · threats (to leave, harm you, harm themselves, or reveal secrets) · controlling money · pressuring for sex or photos · blaming you for their anger.

steps.title: Digital dating abuse
steps.body: Using technology to control or harass: excessive texting/calls, monitoring, stalking via location apps, demanding photos, sharing private images, creating fake profiles, threatening posts. It's abuse, and some actions are crimes (stalking, voyeurism, image sharing without consent).

steps.title: Solved example: care vs control
steps.body:
Care: 'Text me when you get home safe?' (optional, mutual).
Control: 'Share your location always or I'll know you're cheating.'
Care: 'I miss you, have fun with your friends.'
Control: 'If you go, we're done.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing control = protection.
- Sharing passwords 'to prove trust'.
- Thinking only physical violence counts — emotional and digital abuse are abuse too, and affect people of every gender.

statements.s: Demanding live location all the time is a control red flag.
Sharing passwords proves love.
Emotional abuse can be as harmful as physical abuse.
Only women experience relationship abuse.

quiz.q: Checking a partner's phone daily is…
quiz.why: Checking a partner's phone every day is controlling, because it shows distrust and takes away their privacy. Care respects a person's space; it is not required or normal in healthy relationships.
Digital dating abuse means using technology to control or watch a partner, such as stalking through location apps. Sharing memes, goodnight texts and chosen video calls are consensual and healthy.

quiz.q: Threats to self-harm to stop a breakup are…
options: a control tactic — and a safety concern to report
quiz.why: Threatening self-harm to stop a breakup is a control tactic that puts guilt on the partner, and it is also a real safety concern. Tell a trusted adult or helpline so the person gets proper support.
Care supports your freedom, as in 'Have fun with your friends'. Demanding passwords, constant location sharing or ultimatums like 'If you go we're done' are control.
Abuse can affect anyone of any gender or age. Believing it happens only to women, men or adults stops people from seeking help.

lessons.title: Why leaving is hard — and how to get help

scenes.text: After every angry outburst, Neha's boyfriend brings flowers and promises it won't happen again.
It happens again, and again — each time worse.
Her cousin helps her make a safety plan and talk to a counsellor and her family.

steps.title: The cycle of abuse
steps.body: **Tension builds → incident (abuse) → reconciliation (apologies, gifts, promises) → calm ('honeymoon')** → tension builds again. The good phases make it hard to leave and create hope that they'll change.

steps.title: Why people stay
steps.body: Love and hope · fear of what they'll do · threats · shame · isolation from friends · financial dependence · family or social pressure · believing it's their fault. **Leaving can be a risky time**, so planning with support matters.

steps.title: Getting help
steps.body:
- Talk to someone you trust; share what's happening.
- Keep a record (dates, messages) somewhere safe.
- Plan: where to go, who to call, a code word with a friend.
- Services: **112** (danger), **181** (women's helpline), **1098** (under 18), **14416** (mental-health support), One Stop Centres (Sakhi) for women, police, legal aid (DLSA). The **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005** offers protection orders for women in domestic relationships.

steps.title: Solved example: support a friend
steps.body:
- Believe them; don't judge or blame.
- Don't force them to leave — offer support and options.
- Help them find services; offer to go with them.
- If they're in immediate danger → **112**.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

options: part of the cycle, not proof of change
quiz.why: The honeymoon phase, with apologies and gifts, is a part of the cycle of abuse and comes before tension builds again. It isn't proof that the abuser has changed.

options: a risky time — plan with support
quiz.why: Leaving an abusive partner can be a risky time because abusers may escalate when they lose control. So plan with support from trusted people or helplines.
The Women's Helpline number is 181. 108 is the ambulance and 1930 is for cyber fraud.
When a friend tells you about abuse, believe them and support them. Blaming, gossiping or forcing them to leave can make them stop trusting you.
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act (PWDVA) 2005 offers civil remedies such as protection orders. It is not about jobs, school admissions or marriage certificates.

scenes.text: Kabir and Sara decide to break up before college.
They meet in person, are honest and kind, and agree not to post about it.
Both are sad for weeks; friends, sport and time help them heal.

steps.title: Ending a relationship respectfully (and safely)
steps.body:
- If safe, talk in person or by call; be clear and kind: 'I've decided to end this. I care about you, but it's not right for me.'
- Don't blame or list every flaw.
- No public posts or sharing private things.
- **If the relationship is controlling or abusive**, prioritise safety: tell someone, choose a public place or end by message, block if needed.

steps.title: Coping
steps.body: Sadness, anger, relief, confusion — all normal. Helpful: talking to friends, routines, exercise, sleep, limiting checking their profile (mute/unfollow), writing feelings. Unhelpful: revenge, stalking, substances. If low mood lasts 2+ weeks or you feel hopeless → **14416**.

steps.title: Solved example: respecting a breakup
steps.body:
They ended it. You want them back.
- Do: say how you feel once; accept the answer.
- Don't: repeated calls/texts, showing up at their home, threats, posting their secrets — these are harassment and can be crimes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rebound decisions in the first week.
- Making your worth depend on the relationship.
- Ignoring the 'no contact' period you agreed.

activity.prompt: Write three things that would help you through a breakup, and one person you would talk to.
activity.hint: Think: routines, friends, activities, limits on social media.

options: 'I've decided to end this; I care, but it isn't right for me.'
quiz.why: A respectful breakup is clear and kind, such as 'I've decided to end this; I care, but it isn't right for me.' Ghosting with threats, public posts and insults are hurtful.

quiz.q: After an abusive relationship, ending it…
quiz.why: After an abusive relationship, put safety first and tell someone you trust. It doesn't have to be in person or alone, and a public announcement is not needed.

quiz.q: Repeated contact after a clear no:
quiz.why: Repeated contact after a clear no is harassment, because it ignores the person's choice and can cause fear. It is not romance or persistence.
Healthy coping after a breakup includes routines, friends and exercise. Substances, revenge and stalking harm you or others.

quiz.q: Low mood 2+ weeks after a breakup →
quiz.why: Low mood lasting 2+ weeks after a breakup can be depression, so seek support, for example Tele-MANAS 14416. It is not something to ignore or answer with revenge.

questions.why: Healthy relationships are built on respect and equality. Fear, isolation and control are signs of an unhealthy one.
The Women's Helpline number is 181. 1098 is Childline, and 100 alone is just police.

questions.q: Checking a partner's phone daily is…
questions.why: Checking a partner's phone daily is controlling because it shows lack of trust and invades privacy. It isn't care or required.
Jealousy is not proof of love. It often comes from insecurity or a wish to control, and it isn't always healthy.
Demanding passwords is digital dating abuse because it controls a partner's private space. Memes, birthday wishes and chosen video calls are normal.
The cycle of abuse has tension, an incident and a honeymoon phase, where the abuser apologises and is kind before it repeats.

questions.q: Assertion: Leaving an abusive relationship can be risky. Reason: Abusers may escalate when they lose control.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. When abusers lose control they may escalate, which is why leaving can be risky and needs a safety plan.

options: 'Text me when you get home if you like'
questions.why: 'Text me when you get home if you like' shows concern and leaves the choice to you. Banning friends, always sharing location and demanding passwords are control.

options: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act
questions.why: PWDVA stands for the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, passed in 2005. The other options are not real or relevant acts.

questions.q: Case: A friend's partner threatens to share her photos if she leaves. This is…
options: abuse and a crime — help her report
questions.why: Threatening to share someone's photos to stop her leaving is coercion, a form of abuse, and can be a crime. Help her report it and keep evidence.

questions.q: Relationship check score 4/10 with fear present suggests…
questions.why: A low score of 4/10 plus fear is a serious warning, and fear in a relationship always calls for help. Talk to a trusted adult or helpline rather than ignoring it.

questions.q: Why do people stay in abusive relationships?
questions.why: People stay for many reasons like fear, hope the partner will change, isolation, financial or emotional dependence and shame. It is not because they like abuse.

questions.q: Best way to support a friend in an abusive relationship?
options: Believe, offer options and help, don't force
questions.why: Believe your friend, offer options and help, but let them decide. Blaming or ordering them to leave can push them away, and violence makes things more dangerous.

questions.q: Case: After a breakup, he keeps showing up at her college gate. This is…
questions.why: Showing up repeatedly after a breakup is stalking or harassment, which is an offence. It is not romance or persistence.

questions.q: Case: A 17-year-old's partner hits her and says sorry with gifts each time. Best next step?
options: Tell a trusted adult, make a safety plan, contact 1098/181; 112 in danger
questions.why: Hitting followed by gifts is the cycle of abuse, and waiting for change is risky. Tell a trusted adult, make a safety plan and call 1098 or 181, or 112 in danger.

questions.q: Which statement about abuse is TRUE?
options: It can be emotional, digital, sexual, financial or physical
questions.why: Abuse can be emotional, digital, sexual, financial or physical, and it can come from partners, family or others. It is not limited to physical harm, strangers or married people.

questions.q: Which is the safest way to end a controlling relationship?
options: Plan with support; tell someone; public place or message; block if needed
questions.why: The safest way is to plan with support, tell someone, end it by message or in a public place, and block if needed. A secluded meeting is risky, and a public post can provoke the person.

courses.title: Gender, identity & respect
courses.summary: Clear, respectful explanations of sex, gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation; gender stereotypes and how they limit everyone; transgender and intersex people and Indian law; and how to be inclusive and support someone who is questioning or coming out.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish sex, gender identity, gender expression and sexual orientation
Learners can identify and challenge gender stereotypes
Learners can describe transgender and intersex people respectfully and state key Indian legal facts
Learners can respond respectfully to someone's identity and stop identity-based bullying
courses.guardianNote: Introduces sex, gender, gender expression and sexual orientation respectfully and factually; covers stereotypes, transgender and intersex people, Indian legal recognition, inclusion and handling bullying. It does not promote any identity; it promotes respect and safety for everyone (UNESCO ITGSE 2018).

lessons.title: Sex, gender, expression and orientation — the words

scenes.text: In a debate, Kabir realises he's been using 'sex' and 'gender' as if they mean the same.
His teacher lays out four separate ideas on the board.
'So these are different questions about a person,' Kabir says. 'And none of them is my business to guess.'

steps.title: Sex
steps.body: Biological characteristics: chromosomes, hormones, reproductive organs. Usually recorded at birth as female or male. **Intersex** people are born with sex characteristics that don't fit typical definitions — a natural variation.

steps.title: Gender identity
steps.body: A person's inner sense of being a woman, man, both, neither or another gender. For most people it matches their sex assigned at birth (**cisgender**); for **transgender** people it doesn't. India's law recognises transgender persons' right to self-perceived gender identity.

steps.title: Gender expression
steps.body: How someone shows gender outwardly — clothes, hair, voice, mannerisms. Expression doesn't tell you someone's identity or orientation. A boy who dances Kathak or a girl with short hair is just being themselves.

steps.title: Sexual orientation
steps.body: Who someone is emotionally, romantically or sexually attracted to — e.g. heterosexual (straight), gay, lesbian, bisexual, asexual. Orientation is not a choice, not an illness, and cannot be 'cured'; major medical bodies, including WHO, do not classify it as a disorder.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming someone's orientation from how they look or act.
- Using identity words as insults.
- Mixing up intersex and transgender — they are different.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Born with sex traits outside typical definitions
Identity matches sex assigned at birth

quiz.why: Gender expression is how someone shows their gender outwardly, through clothes, hair, behaviour or voice. It is different from biology, name or who they love.
Sexual orientation is not a choice, illness or something catchy. Major medical bodies agree it is a natural part of who a person is.
Intersex refers to natural variations in sex characteristics, such as chromosomes, hormones or anatomy. It is not gender identity, orientation or clothing.

quiz.q: Can you tell orientation by appearance?
quiz.why: No, you can't tell someone's orientation from how they look or act. Appearance is expression, which is different from orientation.

options: gender identity differs from sex assigned at birth
quiz.why: A transgender person's gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth. It is not the same as intersex or same-sex attraction.

lessons.title: Gender stereotypes: how they box everyone in

scenes.text: Aarav loves cooking and wants to join the school cooking club.
Some boys laugh: 'That's for girls.'
He joins anyway. By year-end the club has five boys — and the best biryani at the fest.

steps.title: What stereotypes do
steps.body: Gender stereotypes are fixed ideas about what boys/men and girls/women 'should' be or do: 'boys don't cry', 'girls aren't good at maths', 'men must earn, women must do housework'. They limit choices, mental health (men less likely to seek help) and safety (they feed harassment and violence).

steps.title: Solved example: challenge a stereotype
steps.body:
Statement: 'Girls aren't good at physics.'
- Evidence? Many girls excel; differences in average results largely reflect encouragement and opportunity.
- Who is harmed? Girls who give up; science loses talent.
- Better: 'Anyone can be good at physics with practice and support.'

steps.title: Equality at home and school
steps.body: Share chores regardless of gender; encourage all children in sport, science, arts and care work; use inclusive language ('everyone' instead of 'guys'); call out jokes that demean any gender.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking stereotypes only hurt girls — they hurt boys too.
- Believing 'it's just tradition, so it's harmless'.

items.text: Men should never ask for help
Care work can be done by any gender

quiz.why: Stereotypes are fixed ideas about groups, and they limit everyone by pushing people into narrow roles. They are not facts and affect all genders.
'Boys don't cry' teaches boys to hide feelings, so many men do not seek help for stress or sadness. That harms health.
Inclusive language, like saying 'everyone', includes all genders. 'Guys' only, insults and gender nicknames leave people out or hurt them.

quiz.q: Differences in subject results often reflect…
quiz.why: Differences in subject results by gender mostly reflect encouragement and opportunity, not fixed ability. With equal support, girls and boys do similarly well.

quiz.q: Sharing chores at home should be…
quiz.why: Chores at home should be shared regardless of gender. Assigning them only to girls, mothers or boys reinforces stereotypes.

lessons.title: Transgender and intersex people: facts and Indian law

scenes.text: A transgender student, Priya, joins Class 11 after a school change.
Some classmates ask intrusive questions about her body.
The class teacher explains respectful behaviour: use her name and pronouns, don't ask about her body or medical history, include her.

steps.title: Indian law (topic level)
steps.body:
- **NALSA v. Union of India (2014)**: the Supreme Court recognised transgender persons' right to self-identify their gender, including as 'third gender', and directed protections.
- **Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019**: prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and more; provides for identity certificates.
- **Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)**: consensual sexual relations between adults of the same sex were decriminalised.
- India has a long history of transgender communities, such as hijra and kinnar communities.

steps.title: Respectful behaviour
steps.body: Use the name and pronouns a person uses. Don't ask about their body, surgeries or 'real name'. Don't 'out' anyone (share their identity without permission). Include them in activities. Challenge slurs.

steps.title: Solved example: fix the question
steps.body:
Intrusive: 'What's your real name? Have you had surgery?'
Respectful: 'What name and pronouns should I use?' — or simply treat them like any classmate.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: In 2014 India's Supreme Court recognised the right to self-identify gender.
It's polite to ask a transgender person about surgeries.
The 2019 Act prohibits discrimination against transgender persons.
Outing someone without permission is respectful.

quiz.why: The NALSA v. Union of India judgment, which recognised the right to self-identify gender and a third gender, was delivered in 2014.
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in 2019. 2014 was the NALSA judgment.
Respect means using the name and pronouns a person uses. Asking about surgery, using an old name or outing them is intrusive or harmful.
'Outing' is sharing someone's identity, such as orientation or gender identity, without their permission. It can put them at risk.
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults. It had nothing to do with fees, taxes or traffic.

lessons.title: Being inclusive and supporting someone who comes out

scenes.text: Zubin, 16, messages his best friend: 'I think I might be gay. Please don't tell anyone.'
His friend is surprised, then replies: 'Thanks for trusting me. You're still my best friend.'
Zubin says later, 'That one message made me feel safe.'

steps.title: If someone comes out to you
steps.body:
- Thank them for trusting you.
- Listen; don't make it about you.
- Keep it private — it's their story to share.
- Ask how you can support them.
- Don't say 'It's a phase' or 'Are you sure?'
- If they face bullying, threats or are unsafe at home → help them reach a trusted adult, counsellor, **1098**, **14416**.

steps.title: Questioning is normal
steps.body: Some young people wonder about their identity or attractions. It's okay not to have a label, to take time, or for understanding to develop. Pressure to decide quickly is unnecessary. Mental-health difficulties some LGBTQ+ young people face are linked mainly to **stigma and bullying**, not identity itself.

steps.title: Solved example: respond to a slur
steps.body:
Classmate uses 'gay' as an insult.
- Direct (if safe): 'Not cool using someone's identity as an insult.'
- Distract: change topic.
- Delegate: tell a teacher.
Schools should act on identity-based bullying like any other bullying.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharing the news 'because you care'.
- So-called 'conversion therapy' — attempts to change orientation or identity are harmful and not supported by medical evidence.

a.text: Your friend tells you they're questioning their gender identity and are scared.

choices.label: 'Thanks for telling me. I'm here for you.'
'It's just a phase.'

x.text: Your friend goes quiet. Try again?

choices.label: 'Sorry — that came out wrong. I'm here, whatever you're figuring out.'

b.text: They ask you to keep it private.

choices.label: Keep it private and ask how you can help
Tell a few friends so they can 'help'

c2.text: Your friend is upset that others know.

choices.label: Apologise sincerely and protect their privacy from now on

c.text: Later, someone at school bullies them.

choices.label: Support them and help report it to a teacher

end1.text: Your friend feels safer knowing someone has their back.

quiz.q: When someone comes out, first say…
quiz.why: A supportive first reply is 'Thanks for trusting me.' It shows care. 'It's a phase', 'Are you sure?' or threatening to tell others is dismissive or harmful.

quiz.q: Whose story is it to share?
quiz.why: It is the person's own story, so only they decide when and whom to tell. Sharing it without their permission is outing.

options: harmful and not supported by evidence
quiz.why: Conversion therapy tries to change orientation or gender identity. It is harmful and not supported by evidence, because these are not illnesses to cure.

quiz.q: Higher mental-health difficulties in LGBTQ+ youth are mainly linked to…
quiz.why: Higher mental-health difficulties among LGBTQ+ youth are mainly linked to stigma, rejection and bullying (minority stress), not to identity itself.
Questioning one's identity is okay and normal. It is fine to take time, and it is not wrong or an illness.

questions.why: Sex refers to biological characteristics such as chromosomes, hormones and anatomy. Clothing, name and attraction are separate things.
Gender expression is outward presentation, through clothes, hair, voice and behaviour. It isn't biology, law or attraction.
Stereotypes are over-simple ideas about groups that limit people's choices. They are not facts or laws.
Sexual orientation is who someone is attracted to. Expression is outward presentation, and gender identity is inner sense of gender.
Intersex describes natural variation in sex characteristics. It is not a gender identity, a disease or an orientation.

options: the name and pronouns someone uses
questions.why: Respect means using the name and pronouns a person uses. Slurs, nicknames and old names disrespect their identity.

questions.q: Assertion: You can't tell someone's orientation from appearance. Reason: Expression and orientation are different things.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Expression (how someone looks or acts) is separate from orientation, so appearance can't reveal orientation.

options: self-identification of gender incl. third gender
questions.why: The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised the right to self-identify gender, including a third gender. It was not about marriage, uniforms or voting age.
'Boys shouldn't cry' is a stereotype, a fixed idea about how a group should behave. The other statements are inclusive and not stereotypes.

questions.q: Case: A friend comes out and asks for privacy. Best?
questions.why: When a friend comes out and asks for privacy, keep it private and support them. Telling others, posting or asking parents to be told takes away their choice.

questions.q: Which law prohibits discrimination against transgender persons in education and jobs?
questions.why: The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2019 prohibits discrimination against transgender persons in areas like education and jobs. COTPA and the IT Act deal with other matters.

options: Cisgender – identity matches sex assigned at birth
questions.why: Cisgender means gender identity matches the sex assigned at birth. The other pairs mix up concepts: intersex isn't orientation, and expression isn't biology.

options: It can expose them to discrimination or danger and removes their choice
questions.why: Outing can expose people to discrimination, rejection or danger, and it removes their right to choose when and whom to tell.

questions.q: Case: 'Gay' used as an insult in class. A good upstander response:
options: 'Not cool using identity as an insult' and tell a teacher if it continues
questions.why: A good upstander says calmly that using identity as an insult is not cool and tells a teacher if it continues. Ignoring, laughing or joining makes it acceptable.

options: Sexual orientation is not a disorder and can't be 'cured'
questions.why: Medical consensus, including WHO, is that sexual orientation is not a disorder and cannot be 'cured'. Conversion therapy doesn't work and harms people.

questions.q: Case: A transgender classmate is refused entry to a school event. Which principle applies?
options: Non-discrimination under the 2019 Act and school policy
questions.why: Refusing a transgender student entry is discrimination, which the Transgender Persons Act 2019 and school policy forbid. It is not only up to parents.

questions.q: Which shows challenging a stereotype with evidence?
options: Pointing out many girls excel in physics given support
questions.why: Challenging a stereotype with evidence means pointing to facts, like many girls excelling in physics when supported. Repeating the stereotype, laughing or ignoring doesn't.

courses.title: Adult relationships: communication, POSH at work & talking to children
courses.summary: For young adults and working professionals: communication and conflict skills for couples and families, recognising the 'four destructive patterns', marriage and family pressure (including dowry and consent), sexual harassment at work and the POSH Act 2013, and how parents can talk to children about bodies, consent and safety at each age.
outcomes: Learners can use repair and active-listening skills in close relationships
Learners can recognise destructive conflict patterns and replace them
Learners can describe rights around marriage choice, consent and dowry
Learners can explain the POSH Act process and respond to harassment at work
Learners can plan age-appropriate conversations with children about bodies and safety
courses.guardianNote: Adult course on relationships, workplace harassment (POSH Act 2013) and parenting conversations; non-explicit.

lessons.title: Communication and conflict for couples and families

scenes.text: Every Sunday, Ravi and Meena argue about chores — it always ends in silence.
They try a counsellor's tips: softer starts, listening, taking breaks.
Arguments don't vanish, but they end with a plan instead of a cold war.

steps.title: Four destructive patterns
steps.body:
Relationship researchers describe four patterns that predict trouble:
- **Criticism** (attacking character: 'You're so lazy') → use a **gentle start**: 'I feel overwhelmed with chores; can we plan together?'
- **Contempt** (mockery, eye-rolling) → build **appreciation**.
- **Defensiveness** ('It's not my fault') → **take some responsibility**.
- **Stonewalling** (shutting down) → take a **20-minute break**, calm down, return.

steps.title: Active listening
steps.body: Listen to understand, not to reply. Reflect: 'So you're saying ___; is that right?' Validate feelings even when you disagree: 'I can see why that upset you.'

steps.title: Solved example: rewrite
steps.body:
Criticism: 'You never help, you're useless.'
Gentle start: 'I'm tired after work and the dishes pile up. Could we split them — I'll do weekdays if you do weekends?'
Defensive: 'I was busy!' → Responsible: 'You're right, I've been slack this week. Let's fix it.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Discussing big issues when hungry, tired or angry.
- Bringing in in-laws or past fights.
- Keeping score. Note: if there is fear, violence or control, communication tips are not enough — seek safety and help (181, 112).

activity.prompt: Match the destructive pattern to its antidote

quiz.why: 'You're so lazy' attacks the person's character instead of a specific behaviour, which is criticism. A gentle start-up would describe the problem and your feeling instead.
The antidote to stonewalling is taking a break to calm down and then returning to the talk. Shouting, long silence or leaving forever doesn't resolve it.
Active listening means reflecting back what you heard, so the speaker feels understood. Interrupting, giving advice at once or planning your reply stops real listening.
When there is fear or violence, communication skills are not enough; seek safety and help. Staying quiet or ignoring it can leave the person in danger.
Contempt shows as mockery, sarcasm and eye-rolling, which signal disrespect and superiority. Appreciation, questions and listening are the opposite.

lessons.title: Marriage, family pressure, consent and dowry

scenes.text: At 23, Anjali's family pushes her to marry quickly; she wants to finish her master's.
She explains her plan calmly to her parents, with her aunt's support.
They agree to wait. 'My life, my timing,' she says.

steps.title: Rights (topic level)
steps.body:
- Adults have the right to choose whether, when and whom to marry; consent of both parties is essential.
- **Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006**: minimum age 18 for women, 21 for men.
- **Dowry Prohibition Act 1961**: giving, taking or demanding dowry is an offence; cruelty and dowry-related harassment are also offences under the BNS.
- **Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005**: protection, residence and maintenance orders.
- Within relationships, consent is always required.

steps.title: Handling family pressure
steps.body: Prepare your reasons; choose a calm time; involve a supportive relative; offer a timeline or compromise; seek counselling if conflict is severe. If threatened with violence or forced marriage → **112**, **181**, police, or legal aid (DLSA).

steps.title: Solved example: spot the offence
steps.body:
(a) Groom's family demands a car 'as a gift' → **dowry demand — offence**.
(b) Parents arrange a meeting and the couple decide freely → **fine**.
(c) Marriage of a 16-year-old → **child marriage — prohibited; report to 1098/Child Marriage Prohibition Officer**.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

statements.s: Demanding a car as a wedding 'gift' can be a dowry offence.
Minimum legal marriage age for women in India is 18.
Marriage removes the need for consent.
Forced marriage threats should be reported.

quiz.why: Dowry is prohibited by the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. POSH deals with workplace harassment, COTPA with tobacco and the IT Act with cyber matters.
Under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, the minimum legal marriage age for men is 21 (for women it is 18).
A child marriage should be reported to Childline 1098 or the authorities, who can stop it. Staying silent or posting on social media doesn't protect the child.
Handling family pressure starts with a calm conversation and a plan. Silence, running away or shouting seldom solves it.
The Women's Helpline number is 181. 1098 is Childline, and 1930 is for cyber fraud.

lessons.title: Sexual harassment at work: the POSH Act

scenes.text: At her first job, Divya's manager makes comments about her looks and sends late-night messages.
She documents them and files a written complaint with the Internal Committee.
The IC inquires, the manager faces action, and Divya is protected from retaliation.

steps.title: POSH Act 2013 (Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace)
steps.body:
- Defines sexual harassment broadly: unwelcome physical contact, demands for sexual favours, sexually coloured remarks, showing pornography, and other unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature — including implied promises or threats about the job, and hostile environments.
- Every employer with **10 or more employees** must form an **Internal Committee (IC)** headed by a senior woman employee, with an external member. A **Local Committee** at district level handles other cases.
- Complaint generally within **3 months** of the incident (extendable by up to 3 months for valid reasons).
- Options include **conciliation** (at the complainant's request, not monetary) or **inquiry**; inquiry to be completed within **90 days**.
- **Confidentiality** and protection from victimisation.
- The Act protects women; many organisations extend gender-neutral policies — check yours.

steps.title: What to do
steps.body: Document (dates, messages, witnesses) · tell the harasser clearly if safe ('Stop, this is unwelcome') · file a written complaint with the IC · seek support (HR, colleagues, counsellor) · police complaint for criminal acts under BNS · the government **SHe-Box** portal for complaints.

steps.title: Solved example: is it harassment?
steps.body:
(a) Repeated comments on a colleague's body → **yes**.
(b) 'Promotion if you come to dinner alone' → **yes** (quid pro quo).
(c) A manager giving firm feedback on work quality → **no** (not sexual in nature).
(d) Sharing explicit memes in a team chat → **yes** (hostile environment).

steps.title: Bystanders and managers
steps.body: Speak up or support the target; managers must act on complaints, not discourage them. Retaliation is prohibited.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order the typical POSH complaint process
items: Written complaint to the Internal Committee (generally within 3 months)
IC offers conciliation if requested, or starts inquiry
IC report and action by employer

quiz.q: IC is required for employers with…
quiz.why: The POSH Act requires an Internal Committee (IC) at workplaces with 10 or more employees. Smaller workplaces use a Local Committee.
A complaint is generally to be filed within 3 months of the incident, and the IC can extend this by another 3 months for good reason.
Quid pro quo harassment means offering or tying job benefits, like a promotion, to sexual favours. Firm feedback, lunches and training are normal work.
The POSH inquiry must be completed within 90 days. It should not be left open-ended.
SHe-Box is the Government of India's online portal for complaints of workplace sexual harassment. DigiLocker, IRCTC and UMANG are for other services.

lessons.title: Talking with children about bodies, consent and safety

scenes.text: Five-year-old Ishaan asks, 'Why is my body different from my sister's?'
His father panics, then remembers: calm, simple, correct words.
'Boys have a penis and girls have a vulva. Both are private. Any questions, ask me.' Ishaan nods and goes back to his toy boat.

steps.title: Age-by-age guide
steps.body:
- **0–5**: correct names of body parts; 'your body belongs to you'; safe/unsafe touch; secrets vs surprises; trusted adults.
- **6–9**: privacy; consent in play; basic reproduction ('a baby grows in the uterus'); online rules; puberty is coming.
- **9–12**: puberty in detail for all genders (periods, wet dreams), emotions, friendships, online safety, grooming awareness.
- **13–17**: relationships, consent and the law (18), contraception and STIs factually, sexting risks, pornography myths, where to get help.
This follows UNESCO ITGSE 2018's spiral approach.

steps.title: How to talk
steps.body: Start early and keep it ongoing — many short chats, not one 'big talk'. Stay calm; answer what's asked; it's OK to say 'Great question, let me find out.' Use everyday moments (TV, news, bath time). Model consent: don't force hugs; knock on doors.

steps.title: Solved example: answer a tricky question
steps.body:
Child (7): 'How do babies get inside mummies?'
Simple, accurate answer: 'When grown-ups decide to have a baby, a sperm cell from the man and an egg cell from the woman join together, and the baby grows in the mother's uterus for about nine months.' Then ask: 'Does that answer your question?'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cute nicknames only — correct words help children report abuse.
- Shaming curiosity.
- Waiting until puberty has already begun.
- If a child discloses abuse: stay calm, believe, don't interrogate, reassure, and contact **1098** or police.

activity.prompt: Which age group is this topic usually introduced to? (spiral approach)

items.text: Basic 'a baby grows in the uterus'
Periods and wet dreams in detail

quiz.why: The best approach is many short, ongoing talks as the child grows, which keeps the topic open and normal. A single big talk or leaving it to school leaves gaps.
Teaching correct body-part names helps children report abuse clearly and shows that the body isn't shameful. Vague words can confuse adults.

quiz.q: If you don't know an answer:
quiz.why: If you don't know an answer, honestly say you'll find out and follow up. Making something up spreads myths, and scolding or ignoring shuts down questions.
Puberty talks should begin before puberty starts, so children are prepared, not scared, when changes happen. Waiting until after or until 18 is too late.
When a child discloses abuse, stay calm and believe them. Punishing, ignoring or interrogating can make them stop talking or feel blamed.

questions.why: 'You're so useless' attacks the person, not the behaviour, so it's criticism. A better way is to describe the problem and what you need.
Dowry is an offence under Indian law (Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961). It is not a required custom, legal, or a harmless gift.
The POSH Act (Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act) was passed in 2013. 1961 is the Dowry Prohibition Act and 2005 is PWDVA.
The antidote to defensiveness is taking some responsibility, even for a small part. Attacking back, leaving or going silent escalates the conflict.

questions.q: IC must be formed by employers with…
questions.why: Under the POSH Act, employers with 10 or more employees must form an Internal Committee (IC).

questions.q: Correct names for children's body parts:
questions.why: Correct names for body parts help children stay safe, because they can describe what happened clearly and learn that the body isn't shameful.

questions.q: Assertion: Contempt is especially damaging to relationships. Reason: It communicates disrespect and superiority.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Contempt, such as mockery and eye-rolling, communicates disrespect and superiority, which damages trust and closeness.

options: job benefit tied to sexual favours
questions.why: Quid pro quo means a job benefit, such as promotion, offered in return for sexual favours. It is a form of sexual harassment, unlike feedback or teamwork.
Firm feedback on missed deadlines is ordinary work management and not sexual. Explicit memes, body comments and a promotion for a 'private dinner' are sexual harassment.

questions.q: Case: Groom's family demands cash before wedding. This is…
questions.why: Demanding cash from the bride's side before a wedding is a dowry demand, which is an offence. It isn't a harmless tradition or gift.

questions.q: POSH inquiry must be completed within…
questions.why: A POSH inquiry must be completed within 90 days. It cannot run indefinitely.

options: topics revisited with more depth as children grow
questions.why: The 'spiral' approach in UNESCO's guidance means topics are revisited with more depth as children grow. It isn't a single lesson or biology only.

questions.q: Case: A manager says, 'Don't complain to the IC, it'll ruin your career.' This is…
options: discouraging a complaint/possible victimisation — not allowed
questions.why: Discouraging someone from complaining to the IC, or threatening her career, is victimisation and not allowed. Employees have a right to complain without fear.

questions.q: A 7-year-old asks where babies come from. Best answer style:
questions.why: Answer a 7-year-old simply and accurately, then check what they understood. Myths like storks, refusing or a long lecture don't help.

questions.q: Case: A couple's arguments include eye-rolling and mockery daily. Best change?
options: Replace contempt with appreciation and respectful requests
questions.why: The antidote to contempt is building a culture of appreciation and making respectful requests. Mocking, stonewalling or ignoring keeps the damage going.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about the POSH Act?
questions.why: Under the POSH Act, conciliation cannot involve a monetary settlement. The IC must include women members, and the Act covers all workplaces, with time limits.

questions.q: Case: Your 10-year-old has not heard about periods or wet dreams. Best plan?
options: Start calm, factual talks now, before changes begin
questions.why: Start calm, factual talks now, before changes begin, so your child is prepared. Waiting until 16 or leaving it to friends risks myths and fear.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Relationships
courses.summary: Revise the relationships units — friendships, consent, healthy vs unhealthy relationships, gender & identity, and adult topics — with a facts sheet, case practice and a 20-question mock.
outcomes: Learners can recall key ideas and laws from each unit
Learners can apply consent and respect in new cases
Learners can choose appropriate help
courses.guardianNote: Revision of friendships, consent, healthy relationships, and gender & identity units with practice cases. Non-explicit and respectful.

scenes.text: The life-skills club makes one-page recaps for each unit.
They pin them on the noticeboard.
Even teachers stop to read.

steps.title: Friendship & peer pressure
steps.body: Healthy: respect, trust, be yourself. Refusal: broken record, if–then plans. Conflict: cool down → I-statements → reflect → brainstorm → agree.

steps.title: Consent
steps.body: FRIES. Anything less than a clear yes = stop and check. Intoxication/asleep = no consent. Coercion ≠ consent. Age of consent 18 (POCSO). Digital consent for photos, tags, screenshots.

steps.title: Relationships
steps.body: Spectrum: healthy → unhealthy → abusive. Control red flags; digital dating abuse; cycle of abuse; leaving can be risky — plan with support. 181, 112, 1098, 14416. PWDVA 2005.

steps.title: Gender & adult topics
steps.body: Sex ≠ gender identity ≠ expression ≠ orientation. NALSA 2014; Transgender Persons Act 2019; Navtej 2018. Stereotypes limit all. POSH 2013: IC at 10+ employees, 3-month window, 90-day inquiry. Dowry Act 1961; PCMA 2006 (18/21).

cards.back: Freely given, Reversible, Informed, Enthusiastic, Specific

quiz.why: In FRIES, E stands for Enthusiastic: consent should be a willing yes, not just the absence of a no.
The NALSA judgment, which recognised the right to self-identify gender and a third gender, was delivered in 2014.
The POSH Act requires an Internal Committee in workplaces with 10 or more employees.
The cycle of abuse includes a honeymoon phase, where the abuser apologises and is kind before tension builds again.

scenes.text: Students sit in a circle; each reads a case card.
They discuss the respectful, safe response.
They notice the same ideas keep showing up: respect, consent, safety, help.

steps.title: Case 1
steps.body: A partner demands passwords 'to prove trust' → control red flag; privacy is healthy; talk or seek help.

steps.title: Case 2
steps.body: A friend says 'fine, whatever' after being pushed to go to a party → not freely given; back off.

steps.title: Case 3
steps.body: A classmate is mocked for being 'girly' for dancing → stereotype + bullying; upstander action.

steps.title: Case 4
steps.body: An employee gets 'promotion for dinner' hints → quid pro quo harassment; document; IC complaint.

steps.title: Case 5
steps.body: A friend comes out and asks for privacy → thank, keep private, support.

activity.prompt: Match the case to the key idea

quiz.why: Demanding passwords is control, not love or trust, because it invades privacy. Healthy partners respect each other's private space.
'Fine, whatever' after pressure is not consent because consent must be freely given, and this yes is only to stop the pressure.
Offering a promotion in exchange for dinner ties a job benefit to a personal favour, which is quid pro quo sexual harassment. It is not mentoring or a perk.
When a friend comes out, support them and keep it private. Laughing, questioning or telling others disrespects their trust.

scenes.text: Pairs role-play tough conversations.
Awkward at first, easier by the third try.
'Practising made it feel possible in real life.'

steps.title: Scripts
steps.body:
- Boundary: 'I'm not comfortable with that.'
- Asking: 'Is this OK with you?'
- Respecting a no: 'No worries.'
- Breakup: 'I've decided to end this; I care, but it's not right for me.'
- Coming out support: 'Thanks for trusting me.'
- Harassment: 'Stop. This is unwelcome.'

steps.title: Why scripts work
steps.body: Rehearsed words are easier to reach under stress.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: If you're ever in danger, skip the script — get to safety and call **112**.

activity.text: Asking: 'Is this ___ with you?' Respecting a no: 'No ___.'

quiz.why: 'No worries.' respects the no without pressure. 'You owe me', 'Just once' and 'Why not?!' pressure the person.
Respond to harassment clearly with 'Stop. This is unwelcome.' Laughing or agreeing can seem like acceptance, and ignoring may let it continue.
In danger, get to safety first and call 112, the emergency number. Arguing, waiting or reciting a long script wastes time.

questions.why: A healthy friend respects your no. Mocking, controlling or isolating you are signs of an unhealthy friendship.
The age of consent in India is 18, and under POCSO anyone below 18 is a child.
The Women's Helpline number is 181. 1098 is Childline and 1930 is for cyber fraud.
Stereotypes limit everyone by squeezing them into narrow roles. They are not facts or laws.
Silence is not a yes, because consent needs a clear sign of agreement. Not saying no does not mean saying yes.
Checking a partner's phone daily is control because it shows distrust and takes away privacy. It isn't trust or care.
Gender expression is how a person presents their gender outwardly. It isn't biology, law or attraction.
The POSH Act was passed in 2013. 1961 is the Dowry Prohibition Act, 2005 is PWDVA and 2019 is the Transgender Persons Act.

questions.q: Assertion: Intoxicated people cannot consent. Reason: They lack capacity to make a free, informed choice.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. An intoxicated person lacks the capacity to make a free, informed choice, so cannot give valid consent.

questions.q: The cycle of abuse's calm phase is…
questions.why: The calm phase in the cycle of abuse is the honeymoon phase. It is not proof of change, because tension often builds again.
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was passed in 2019. 2014 was the NALSA judgment.
The antidote to stonewalling is a break to calm down, followed by returning to the talk. Shouting, silence or leaving forever doesn't help.

questions.q: Case: A friend agreed to a photo but not to posting it. You…
questions.why: Consent is specific: agreeing to a photo isn't agreeing to posting it. So don't post, tag or forward it.

questions.q: Case: Groom's family demands a bike. This is…
questions.why: Demanding a bike from the bride's family is a dowry demand, which is an offence. It is not a gift or harmless tradition.
A POSH complaint is generally to be made within 3 months of the incident, extendable by up to 3 more months.

questions.q: Case: A classmate's identity is shared without consent. This is…
questions.why: Sharing someone's identity without their consent is outing, and it can cause discrimination or danger. It is not news or support.

questions.q: Case: Partner says 'If you loved me you'd send a photo.' Best?
options: Refuse; it's pressure; consider the relationship's health
questions.why: 'If you loved me you'd send a photo' is emotional pressure, not real consent. Refuse, and think about whether the relationship is healthy; never send or share passwords to prove love.

questions.q: Which reflects the spiral approach for parents?
options: Revisit topics with more depth as children grow
questions.why: The spiral approach means revisiting topics with more depth as children grow, rather than one talk or only biology at 18.

questions.q: Why can leaving an abusive relationship be risky?
options: Abusers may escalate when losing control
questions.why: Leaving can be risky because abusers may escalate when they lose control, so a safety plan and support are important.

options: Sexual orientation is not a choice or illness
questions.why: Sexual orientation is not a choice or an illness. Expression isn't orientation, orientation isn't visible and conversion therapy doesn't work.

well-reproductive.title: Reproductive & sexual health: facts for life
well-reproductive.description: Human reproduction (board/NEET level), contraception, STIs and HIV, pregnancy, safe-abortion law, fertility and adult sexual health — clinical, factual, non-explicit and judgment-free.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Human reproduction: systems, gametes, fertilisation & birth
