courses.summary: Exam-ready biology of human reproduction: male and female reproductive systems, spermatogenesis and oogenesis, hormonal control of the menstrual cycle, fertilisation and implantation, placenta, pregnancy and parturition, and lactation — with solved problems.
outcomes: Learners can label and describe the male and female reproductive systems
Learners can compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis including ploidy
Learners can explain hormonal control of the menstrual cycle
Learners can describe fertilisation, implantation and placental functions
Learners can outline pregnancy, parturition and lactation
courses.guardianNote: Biology of human reproduction at Class 10–12 level (reproductive systems, gametogenesis, menstrual cycle, fertilisation, pregnancy and birth), clinical and non-explicit, as taught in senior-secondary biology.

scenes.text: In Class 12 biology, Om labels a diagram of the male reproductive system.
His teacher asks him to trace sperm from the testis to the outside — and name each gland's job.
He realises each part makes sense once he follows the path.

steps.title: Parts and functions
steps.body:
- **Testes** (in the scrotum, 2–2.5 °C below body temperature): each has ~250 compartments (**testicular lobules**) containing **seminiferous tubules** lined by spermatogonia and **Sertoli cells** (nourish developing sperm). **Leydig (interstitial) cells** between tubules secrete **testosterone**.
- **Rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis** (sperm mature and are stored) **→ vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra**.
- **Accessory glands**: **seminal vesicles** (fructose-rich fluid for energy), **prostate** (alkaline fluid), **bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands** (lubricating mucus). Their secretions + sperm = **semen**.

steps.title: Solved example: trace the path
steps.body:
Q: Write the path of sperm.
A: Seminiferous tubules → rete testis → vasa efferentia → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra → urethral meatus.

Q: Why is the scrotum outside? A: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature ~2–2.5 °C lower than core body temperature.

steps.title: Solved example: function match
steps.body: Fructose → seminal vesicle (energy for sperm motility). Testosterone → Leydig cells. Nourishment of germ cells → Sertoli cells.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping Sertoli (nourish) and Leydig (hormone).
- Writing 'vas deferens stores sperm' — the **epididymis** is the main storage/maturation site.
- Forgetting the urethra is shared by urinary and reproductive systems in males.

quiz.why: Leydig (interstitial) cells between the seminiferous tubules secrete testosterone under LH. Sertoli cells support sperm, and the epididymis and prostate have other roles.
Sertoli cells are 'nurse cells' in the seminiferous tubules that nourish and support developing sperm. They do not store urine, make fructose or secrete LH.
The seminal vesicles add fructose to semen, which gives sperm energy. The prostate adds other fluid, and the testis makes sperm.
Sperm mature and gain motility mainly in the epididymis, where they are also stored. The prostate and urethra do not mature sperm.

quiz.q: Scrotal temperature is lower by about…
quiz.why: The scrotum is about 2–2.5 °C cooler than core body temperature, which suits sperm production. 5–8 °C is too much.

scenes.text: Sana studies a 3D model of the female reproductive system.
She notices the fimbriae — finger-like edges — near the ovary.
'So they catch the egg after ovulation!' She connects structure to function.

steps.title: Parts and functions
steps.body:
- **Ovaries** (pair, almond-sized): produce **ova** and hormones (**oestrogen, progesterone**). Contain follicles at different stages.
- **Fallopian tubes (oviducts)**: **infundibulum** with **fimbriae** (collect the ovum) → **ampulla** (usual site of **fertilisation**) → **isthmus** → uterus.
- **Uterus**: wall layers — **perimetrium** (outer), **myometrium** (thick smooth muscle; contracts in birth), **endometrium** (inner glandular lining; changes every cycle).
- **Cervix** (narrow lower uterus) opens into the **vagina** (birth canal).
- **External genitalia (vulva)**: mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoris, openings of urethra and vagina. The hymen is a thin membrane that varies greatly; it is **not** a reliable sign of anything.
- **Mammary glands**: milk-producing alveoli → ducts → nipple.

steps.title: Solved example: sites
steps.body:
Q: Site of fertilisation? → **Ampulla** of the fallopian tube.
Q: Site of implantation? → **Endometrium** of the uterus.
Q: Which layer contracts during labour? → **Myometrium**.

steps.title: Solved example: count gametes
steps.body: A female is born with roughly **1–2 million** primary follicles; by puberty about **60,000–80,000** remain (NCERT figure); only ~**400–500** ova are released over a reproductive lifetime (about one per cycle × ~13 cycles/year × ~35–40 years).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Fertilisation 'in the uterus' — it is in the **ampulla**.
- Mixing myometrium and endometrium.
- Myths about the hymen and 'virginity tests' — medically meaningless and WHO calls them a human-rights violation.

pairs: Narrow lower part of uterus opening to vagina

quiz.why: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla, the widest part of the fallopian tube. The uterus is where the embryo implants.
Implantation occurs in the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus. The myometrium is the muscle layer and the perimetrium the outer covering.
Oestrogen is made mainly by the ovary (follicle cells). The uterus, cervix and vagina respond to hormones but don't make oestrogen.
The vagina is the birth canal through which the baby is born. The cervix is only its upper opening, and the fallopian tube and ovary are higher up.

options: medically meaningless and a rights violation
quiz.why: 'Virginity tests' have no medical basis, since the hymen varies and can change without sex, and they violate rights, as WHO says. They are neither reliable nor required.

lessons.title: Gametogenesis and the menstrual cycle hormones

scenes.text: Before NEET mock tests, Rhea keeps confusing n and 2n in gametogenesis.
She draws two ladders side by side: sperm and egg.
Now she can answer any 'how many chromosomes at this stage' question.

steps.title: Spermatogenesis (from puberty, in seminiferous tubules)
steps.body: Spermatogonium (2n=46) → mitosis → **primary spermatocyte (2n)** → meiosis I → **2 secondary spermatocytes (n=23)** → meiosis II → **4 spermatids (n)** → **spermiogenesis** → **4 sperm (n)**. Triggered by **GnRH → LH (acts on Leydig cells → testosterone) and FSH (acts on Sertoli cells)**.

steps.title: Oogenesis (begins before birth)
steps.body: Oogonia (2n) → **primary oocytes (2n)** arrested in prophase I **before birth** → at puberty, each cycle one completes meiosis I → **secondary oocyte (n) + first polar body** → ovulated at metaphase II → meiosis II completes **only if a sperm enters** → **ovum (n) + second polar body**. One primary oocyte → **1 ovum** (+ polar bodies).

steps.title: Hormones of the cycle
steps.body:
- **Follicular phase**: FSH → follicle growth → **oestrogen** rises → endometrium proliferates.
- **Mid-cycle LH surge** → **ovulation** (~day 14 of a 28-day cycle).
- **Luteal phase**: ruptured follicle becomes **corpus luteum** → **progesterone** (maintains endometrium).
- No fertilisation → corpus luteum degenerates → progesterone falls → **menstruation**.
- Pregnancy → embryo makes **hCG**, keeping the corpus luteum alive.

steps.title: Solved example: numbers
steps.body:
(a) 100 primary spermatocytes → **400 sperm**.
(b) 100 primary oocytes → **100 ova** (and polar bodies).
(c) Chromosomes in a secondary spermatocyte: **23**. In a primary oocyte: **46**.
(d) Cycle of 30 days → ovulation about day **16**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the ovum is released after meiosis II — it's released as a **secondary oocyte** arrested at metaphase II.
- Forgetting polar bodies.
- Mixing roles of LH (ovulation, Leydig cells) and FSH (follicle growth, Sertoli cells).

activity.prompt: How many sperm are produced from 250 primary spermatocytes?

quiz.why: A primary spermatocyte (2n = 46) divides by meiosis I into two secondary spermatocytes, each haploid (n = 23). So its ploidy is n.
A surge of LH (luteinising hormone) from the pituitary triggers ovulation. Prolactin starts milk production, and hCG comes from the embryo.
The corpus luteum, formed from the ruptured follicle, mainly secretes progesterone, which prepares the endometrium for pregnancy. Oxytocin, LH and FSH are made elsewhere.

quiz.q: 50 primary oocytes give how many ova?
quiz.why: Oogenesis gives only one ovum per primary oocyte, as the other cells become polar bodies. So 50 primary oocytes give 50 ova.

quiz.q: Meiosis II in the oocyte completes…
quiz.why: The secondary oocyte stays arrested in metaphase II after ovulation, and meiosis II completes only after a sperm enters. So fertilisation triggers it.

scenes.text: A doctor shows a video of an embryo dividing in an IVF lab.
'Every human started as one cell — a zygote,' she says.
The class follows its journey down the fallopian tube to implantation.

steps.title: Fertilisation
steps.body: During sexual intercourse, semen is deposited in the vagina; sperm swim through the cervix and uterus to the fallopian tube. One sperm penetrates the zona pellucida of the secondary oocyte in the **ampulla**; this triggers meiosis II and blocks other sperm. Nuclei fuse → **zygote (2n)**. Sex is determined by the sperm: X sperm → **XX (female)**, Y sperm → **XY (male)** — the egg always carries X.

steps.title: Cleavage and implantation
steps.body: Zygote divides as it moves down the tube (cleavage) → **morula** (8–16 cells) → **blastocyst** (outer **trophoblast** + inner cell mass). Around **day 6–7** the blastocyst **implants** in the endometrium. The inner cell mass becomes the embryo; the trophoblast helps form the **placenta**.

steps.title: Placenta
steps.body: Connects embryo to uterine wall via the **umbilical cord**. Functions: exchange of oxygen, nutrients, CO₂ and wastes (blood of mother and foetus do **not** mix directly); acts as an endocrine organ — **hCG, hPL, oestrogen, progesterone** (and relaxin later in pregnancy). Some substances (alcohol, nicotine, some drugs, some infections) cross it — why prenatal care matters.

steps.title: Solved example: probability of sex
steps.body: Each pregnancy: sperm X or Y with ~equal chance → **50% girl, 50% boy**, independent of previous children. Family with 3 daughters — chance the 4th child is a boy? Still **½**. The father's sperm determines sex; blaming mothers for a child's sex is scientifically wrong. (Sex-selection and prenatal sex determination are banned in India under the PCPNDT Act.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Mother decides the baby's sex' — the sperm does.
- 'Maternal and foetal blood mix in the placenta' — they don't directly.
- Mixing morula and blastocyst.

items: Secondary oocyte enters the fallopian tube
Sperm fertilises it in the ampulla

quiz.q: The sex of a baby is determined by…
quiz.why: The father's sperm decides the baby's sex, since it carries either X or Y while the egg always carries X. XX gives a girl and XY a boy.
The blastocyst implants in the endometrium about 6–7 days after fertilisation. Day 1 is too early and day 30 too late.
Pregnancy tests detect hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin), made by the embryo's cells after implantation. Insulin, FSH and LH are not the marker.

quiz.q: Placenta: do maternal and foetal blood mix directly?
quiz.why: No, maternal and foetal blood do not mix directly. Exchange of nutrients, gases and waste takes place across the placental barrier by diffusion and transport.

quiz.q: India's law banning prenatal sex determination:
quiz.why: The PCPNDT Act (Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act) bans prenatal sex determination. COTPA is about tobacco, POSH about harassment and the IT Act about cyber matters.

scenes.text: At a primary health centre, a mother-to-be gets her first antenatal check-up.
The nurse estimates the due date and schedules iron-folic acid tablets and tests.
Nine months later, labour begins — her body's hormones take over.

steps.title: Pregnancy
steps.body: Human pregnancy lasts about **9 months (~40 weeks from the last menstrual period, ~38 weeks from conception)**. By end of 1st month the heart forms; by end of 2nd month limbs and digits; by end of 1st trimester most organ systems; first movements around the 5th month. **Antenatal care**: regular check-ups, iron–folic acid, tetanus vaccination, tests, nutrition, no alcohol/tobacco.

steps.title: Parturition and lactation
steps.body: **Parturition** (birth) is triggered by signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta → **foetal ejection reflex** → **oxytocin** from the posterior pituitary → strong **myometrium** contractions (positive feedback) → birth. **Lactation**: **prolactin** stimulates milk production; oxytocin causes milk let-down. **Colostrum** (first milk) is rich in antibodies (**IgA**) — WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months.

steps.title: Solved example: due date (Naegele's rule)
steps.body:
LMP = 10 March. Add 1 year, subtract 3 months, add 7 days → **17 December**. (An estimate — ultrasound refines it.)

Second: LMP 1 June → 1 June − 3 months = 1 March, + 7 days = **8 March** (next year).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling oxytocin's loop negative feedback — labour contractions are **positive feedback**.
- Thinking colostrum should be discarded — it's protective.
- Teen pregnancy carries higher risks; legal and safe options and support exist (see Unit 4).

activity.prompt: Match the hormone to its role
pairs: Maintains corpus luteum early in pregnancy
Softens pelvic ligaments late in pregnancy

quiz.why: Oxytocin drives the contractions of labour. FSH, insulin and thyroxine do not do this.
Colostrum, the first milk, is rich in antibodies, especially IgA, which give the newborn passive immunity. It is not just fat or sugar.
WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life, with other foods added after that.
Naegele's rule: take LMP, subtract 3 months, then add 7 days. 20 January − 3 months = 20 October, + 7 days = 27 October.
Labour is a positive feedback loop: contractions push the baby against the cervix, which signals more oxytocin and more contractions until birth. Negative feedback would reverse a change.

questions.why: Fertilisation takes place in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, the widest part. The uterus is where implantation occurs.
Leydig cells in the testis make testosterone. Sertoli cells nourish sperm, and the prostate and seminal vesicles add fluids.
Pregnancy tests detect hCG, a hormone made by the embryo's cells after implantation. Insulin, FSH and LH aren't used as the marker.
The embryo implants in the endometrium, the uterine lining. The myometrium is the muscle layer, and the cervix and tube are not sites of implantation.
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary stimulates milk production. Oxytocin triggers milk ejection, not production.
Sperm get energy from fructose in the fluid added by the seminal vesicles. Urine glucose, protein only and starch are not their energy source.

questions.q: Assertion: The father's sperm determines the baby's sex. Reason: Eggs always carry an X chromosome.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Eggs always carry an X, so the sperm's X or Y decides whether the baby is a girl or boy.
The corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which maintains the endometrium. Oxytocin, FSH and prolactin come from other sources.

options: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I before birth
questions.why: Primary oocytes form before birth and are arrested in prophase I until puberty. Oogenesis gives one ovum, not four, and completes only after fertilisation.

questions.q: Case: A family blames the mother for having daughters only. Scientific response?
options: The sperm determines sex; each child's chance is ~50%
questions.why: The sperm decides sex, since eggs always carry X, and each pregnancy has about a 50% chance of a girl or boy. So blaming the mother is unscientific.
Each primary spermatocyte gives 4 sperm through meiosis. So 200 × 4 = 800 sperm.
A spermatid is haploid, with 23 chromosomes, after meiosis. 46 is diploid and 92 is after DNA replication in a dividing cell.
Naegele's rule: subtract 3 months, add 7 days. 5 April − 3 months = 5 January, + 7 days = 12 January.

questions.q: Ovulation day in a 32-day cycle (luteal 14 days):
questions.why: Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period (the luteal phase). So in a 32-day cycle, 32 − 14 = day 18.

questions.q: Why does menstruation occur if fertilisation doesn't happen?
options: Corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, endometrium sheds
questions.why: If no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum degenerates, progesterone falls, and the endometrium sheds as menstruation. A rise in hCG would actually maintain pregnancy.
Implantation takes place in the endometrium, not the myometrium. The myometrium is the muscle layer that contracts during labour.

questions.q: Why is labour an example of positive feedback?
options: Contractions trigger more oxytocin release, increasing contractions until birth
questions.why: In labour, contractions trigger more oxytocin release, which causes stronger contractions, and this continues until birth. That amplifying loop is positive feedback.

questions.q: Which substance can cross the placenta and harm the foetus?
options: Red blood cells of mother in bulk
questions.why: Alcohol crosses the placenta and can harm the foetus (it is a teratogen). Large proteins and bulk maternal red cells normally do not cross.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Contraception: how methods work, effectiveness & myths
courses.summary: A complete factual guide: why contraception matters, barrier methods, hormonal methods (pills, injectables), IUDs, permanent methods, emergency contraception, effectiveness with typical use, side effects, myths, and free services in India — for knowledge and future life.
outcomes: Learners can classify contraceptive methods by how they work
Learners can compare methods using typical-use effectiveness
Learners can explain emergency contraception and its time window
Learners can correct common myths
Learners can name where to get free services and counselling in India
courses.guardianNote: Factual, non-explicit information on how contraceptive methods work, their effectiveness and side effects, emergency contraception, myths and where to get services in India. Taught for knowledge and health; it reminds learners that the age of consent in India is 18 and that delaying sexual activity is a valid choice.

lessons.title: Why contraception matters, and the big picture

scenes.text: In a senior-school health class, the teacher shows a chart on family planning from national health surveys.
'Why do people use contraception?' she asks.
The class lists: spacing children, preventing unintended pregnancy, protecting health, education and career plans — and condoms also prevent STIs.

steps.title: What contraception is
steps.body: **Contraception** means methods used to prevent pregnancy. It supports health (safer spacing between births), education and life plans, and — for condoms — protection from **sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**. Choosing **not** to have sex (abstinence) is also 100% effective and a valid choice at any age. In India the **age of consent is 18**.

steps.title: Ways methods work
steps.body:
- **Barrier**: stop sperm meeting the egg (male & female condoms, diaphragm).
- **Hormonal**: mainly stop ovulation and thicken cervical mucus (combined pill, progestin-only pill, injectables, implants, hormonal IUD).
- **IUDs**: placed in the uterus by a trained provider (copper IUD such as Copper-T; hormonal IUD).
- **Permanent**: tubectomy (female), vasectomy (male).
- **Emergency contraception**: after unprotected sex or method failure.
- **Fertility-awareness and withdrawal**: less reliable.

steps.title: Solved example: perfect vs typical use
steps.body: 'Typical use' includes real-life mistakes (missed pills, late injections, condom slips). If a method has a **13%** typical-use failure rate, out of **100** couples using it for a year, about **13** experience a pregnancy. If failure is **0.8%** (copper IUD), about **1 in 125**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up STI protection and pregnancy prevention — **only condoms** do both.
- Thinking contraception causes infertility later — most methods are fully reversible (fertility returns, sometimes after a delay with injectables).

quiz.q: Which method also protects against STIs?
quiz.why: Condoms are a barrier method, so they also protect against many STIs. Pills, vasectomy and Copper-T prevent pregnancy but not infections.
Typical use means how a method works in real life, including mistakes like missed doses. Perfect use is the best-case figure.
A 13% failure rate means about 13 pregnancies per 100 couples using the method for a year.
Abstinence is a valid choice and is 100% effective against pregnancy if followed. It is neither illegal nor unsafe.
Most contraception is reversible, so fertility returns after stopping. Only sterilisation is meant to be permanent.

scenes.text: At a college health camp, a counsellor demonstrates condom facts on a model (no explicit content).
Students ask anonymous questions: 'Can it break? Does it expire?'
They learn correct use matters as much as the method.

steps.title: Male and female (internal) condoms
steps.body: Thin latex or polyurethane sheaths that collect semen / line the vagina. **Typical-use effectiveness: male condom ~87%, internal condom ~79%**; much higher with correct, consistent use. **Protect against STIs including HIV.** Free **Nirodh** condoms are available at government health facilities; also sold in pharmacies.

steps.title: Correct-use checklist (non-explicit)
steps.body:
- Check the **expiry date** and that the packet isn't damaged.
- Open carefully (no teeth or scissors).
- Use a **new condom every time**, from start to finish.
- Use **water- or silicone-based lubricant** with latex — oil-based (coconut oil, Vaseline) can weaken latex.
- **Never use two condoms together** (friction can tear them).
- Store away from heat (not for months in a wallet).
- If one breaks or slips → consider **emergency contraception** and STI testing.

steps.title: Solved example: spot the errors
steps.body:
Scenario: an old condom from a wallet, used with coconut oil, two at once 'for safety'.
Errors: (1) heat/friction damage in wallet, (2) oil weakens latex, (3) double-bagging increases tearing. → **Fix**: fresh condom, water-based lube, one at a time.

steps.title: Common myths
steps.body:
- 'Condoms reduce pleasure so much they're useless' — many sizes and types exist.
- 'Only men buy condoms' — anyone can.
- 'Condoms are 100%' — high but not perfect; consistent use is key.

statements.s: Oil-based lubricants can weaken latex condoms.
Using two condoms at once is safer.
Condoms protect against HIV.
Condoms can be reused if washed.
Free condoms are available at government health centres.

quiz.q: Typical-use effectiveness of male condoms is about…
quiz.why: Male condoms are about 87% effective with typical use (about 13% failure), and about 98% with perfect use. 100% is not realistic.
Use water-based (or silicone) lubricant with latex condoms. Oils like Vaseline, coconut oil or butter weaken latex and can cause breakage.

options: consider emergency contraception and STI testing
quiz.why: If a condom breaks, consider emergency contraception as soon as possible and get STI testing. Washing or using another later does not prevent pregnancy or infection.

options: in a hot wallet for months
quiz.why: Store condoms away from heat, in a cool dry place. Sun, a hot wallet or freezing can damage them.
Nirodh is the free condom brand supplied by the Indian government. Mala-N is a pill and Antara an injectable.

scenes.text: Married at 24, Pooja visits a government health centre to discuss spacing her first child.
The counsellor explains pills, the 3-monthly injectable, Copper-T and the weekly non-hormonal pill — with pros and side effects.
Pooja chooses after discussing with her husband. 'An informed choice — my choice.'

steps.title: Pills
steps.body:
- **Combined oral contraceptive pill (COC)** — oestrogen + progestin; taken daily; stops ovulation. Typical use ~**93%** effective. Available free as **Mala-N** at government facilities. Not suitable for some people (e.g. certain migraines, clotting risk, smokers over 35) — needs a health check.
- **Progestin-only pill** — suitable during breastfeeding.
- **Centchroman (Chhaya)** — a **non-hormonal weekly pill** available in India's public programme.

steps.title: Injectables and implants
steps.body: **DMPA injectable** (government brand **Antara**) every **3 months**; typical use ~**96%**. Periods may become irregular or stop (reversible). Return of fertility can take several months after stopping. **Implants** (rod under the arm skin, >99%) exist worldwide; availability in India is more limited.

steps.title: IUDs (intrauterine devices)
steps.body: Small T-shaped devices placed in the uterus by a trained provider. **Copper IUD (Copper-T 380A, ~10 years; Cu-375, ~5 years)**: copper is toxic to sperm; **>99%** effective; can make periods heavier at first. **Hormonal IUD (LNG-IUS)**: lighter periods; ~5 years. Fertility returns quickly after removal. Can be inserted after childbirth (PPIUCD) in government hospitals.

steps.title: Solved example: compare yearly failures (per 1,000 users, typical use)
steps.body:
Pill 7% → **70**. Injectable 4% → **40**. Copper IUD 0.8% → **8**. Condom 13% → **130**. Withdrawal 20% → **200**.
Lesson: long-acting methods (IUD, implant) have the lowest failure because they don't depend on daily actions.

steps.title: Common myths
steps.body:
- 'The pill makes you infertile' — fertility returns after stopping.
- 'Copper-T travels to the heart/brain' — impossible; rarely it can move within or perforate the uterus, which providers check for.
- 'Hormonal methods cause cancer' — combined pills slightly change some risks but **lower** risks of ovarian and endometrial cancer; discuss individually with a doctor.
- 'Pills protect from STIs' — no.

activity.prompt: Match the method to the right fact
pairs: Copper IUD lasting up to ~10 years

quiz.why: Antara is an injectable (DMPA) given every 3 months, so it needs no daily action.
The copper IUD is over 99% effective, since it needs no daily action and the copper is toxic to sperm.
Chhaya (centchroman) is a non-hormonal oral contraceptive taken weekly. Antara is hormonal injectable, Mala-N is a daily hormonal pill and Nirodh is a condom.

quiz.q: Pill at 7% typical failure: per 1,000 users/year:
quiz.why: 7% of 1,000 users is 0.07 × 1,000 = 70 pregnancies per year.
Long-acting methods like IUDs have the lowest typical failure because they don't depend on daily or per-act use. Condoms, withdrawal and awareness methods rely on correct use every time.

scenes.text: A married couple's condom slips. They're anxious.
At a pharmacy they learn about the emergency contraceptive pill and that sooner is better.
Later, they discuss long-term options with a doctor.

steps.title: Emergency contraception (EC)
steps.body:
- **Levonorgestrel EC pill**: take as soon as possible, ideally within **72 hours (3 days)** of unprotected sex — the sooner the more effective. It mainly **delays ovulation**. It is **not an abortion pill** and won't end an established pregnancy. Sold at pharmacies in India.
- **Copper IUD** inserted within **5 days** is the **most effective** EC.
- EC is for emergencies, not regular contraception; doesn't protect from STIs.

steps.title: Permanent methods
steps.body:
- **Tubectomy** (female sterilisation): fallopian tubes are blocked/cut; minor surgery.
- **Vasectomy** (male sterilisation): vas deferens cut/tied; simpler and safer than tubectomy, does **not** affect strength, erection or masculinity; needs back-up contraception until a semen test confirms no sperm (often ~3 months). Both are meant to be permanent; reversal is difficult and not guaranteed. Free under government programmes, with compensation schemes.

steps.title: Solved example: EC timing
steps.body: Unprotected sex Monday 11 pm. 72-hour window ends **Thursday 11 pm**. Best: take EC pill on Tuesday morning (sooner = better). Copper IUD window: up to **Saturday 11 pm** (5 days).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Waiting till the last hour of the window.
- Using EC repeatedly instead of a regular method.
- Believing vasectomy causes weakness — it doesn't.
- If periods are over a week late after EC → pregnancy test.

activity.prompt: An emergency contraceptive pill is best taken within how many hours of unprotected sex (standard window)?

quiz.why: A copper IUD inserted within 5 days is the most effective emergency contraception. An EC pill on day 6 is too late for reliable effect, and waiting does nothing.
The EC pill mainly works by delaying ovulation so there is no egg when sperm are present. It does not end an existing pregnancy or prevent STIs.
Vasectomy does not affect strength, erections or sexual drive, so the fear of weakness is a myth. It only blocks the passage of sperm.

quiz.q: Unprotected sex Fri 10 pm: EC pill window ends…
quiz.why: The standard EC pill window is 72 hours. 72 h after Friday 10 pm is Monday 10 pm (Sat, Sun, Mon).

quiz.q: After vasectomy, back-up is needed until…
quiz.why: After vasectomy, sperm remain in the tubes for some time, so use back-up until a semen test shows no sperm. Early unprotected sex can still cause pregnancy.

lessons.title: Myths, rights and where to get help

scenes.text: An ASHA worker hears many myths: 'Copper-T causes cancer', 'pills make you weak', 'men lose strength with vasectomy'.
She answers each calmly with facts and invites families to the health centre.
More couples choose a method that suits them.

steps.title: Where to get services in India
steps.body: Government sub-centres, PHCs, CHCs and district hospitals (free condoms, pills, Antara, Chhaya, IUDs, sterilisation, counselling); **ASHA** workers deliver supplies at home; pharmacies sell condoms, pills and EC; private clinics. Adolescent-friendly health clinics (**AFHCs**) under the **Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram (RKSK)** offer confidential counselling for teens.

steps.title: Rights and consent
steps.body: Contraceptive choice should be **voluntary and informed**; no one should be pressured or forced. Both partners share responsibility. Health workers should maintain privacy.

steps.title: Solved example: myth or fact?
steps.body:
(a) 'Pills cause permanent infertility' → **myth**.
(b) 'Condoms protect from HIV' → **fact**.
(c) 'You can't get pregnant the first time' → **myth**.
(d) 'Withdrawal is very reliable' → **myth** (~20% typical failure).
(e) 'EC is an abortion pill' → **myth**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Getting information from friends or porn instead of health workers; assuming one method suits everyone.

activity.prompt: Questions people hesitate to ask about contraception

items.q: Can you get pregnant the first time?
items.a: Yes. Pregnancy can happen any time sperm meets an egg.

items.q: Can you get pregnant during a period?
items.a: Less likely, but possible — especially with short cycles.

items.q: Do pills make you gain lots of weight?
items.a: Large studies show little average weight change; individuals vary.

items.q: Is it embarrassing to ask a pharmacist?
items.a: Pharmacists answer these questions daily and should keep it private.

items.q: Do teens have access to counselling?
items.a: Adolescent-friendly health clinics (RKSK) offer confidential counselling.

quiz.why: Yes, pregnancy is possible the first time. Ovulation can occur at any time, so the first intercourse isn't safe.
Withdrawal has a typical failure rate of about 20%, because sperm can be in pre-ejaculate and timing is hard. It is unreliable.
RKSK (Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram) runs adolescent-friendly health clinics giving counselling and services to young people.
Contraceptive choice must be voluntary and informed, a matter of reproductive rights. Forced use or decisions by neighbours violate this.

options: deliver supplies and advice at home
quiz.why: ASHA workers are community health workers who deliver supplies and advice at home. They are not police or teachers.

questions.q: Only method that also prevents STIs:
questions.why: Condoms are the barrier that also protect against many STIs. IUDs, pills and vasectomy only prevent pregnancy.
Antara is an injectable contraceptive (DMPA) given every 3 months. It isn't a condom, pill or IUD.
The standard EC pill window is 72 hours (3 days) after unprotected sex, and it works better the earlier it is taken.
Copper-T is an intrauterine device (IUD) placed in the uterus. It is not a pill, condom or injectable.
Avoid oil-based lubricants with latex condoms, because oil weakens latex and can cause the condom to break.
Vasectomy is male sterilisation, where the vas deferens are cut or blocked. Female sterilisation is tubectomy.

questions.q: Assertion: Long-acting methods have low typical failure. Reason: They don't rely on daily user action.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Long-acting methods don't rely on daily action, so there are fewer user errors and lower typical failure.
The combined pill mainly works by stopping ovulation through hormones. Copper acts as an IUD, a barrier is a condom, and blocking tubes is sterilisation.
Chhaya contains centchroman, a non-hormonal contraceptive pill taken weekly. It is not a condom, IUD or injectable.

questions.q: Case: Condom slipped Saturday night. Best step?
options: EC as soon as possible and consider STI test
questions.why: After a slipped condom, take emergency contraception as soon as possible and consider an STI test. Waiting two weeks or doing nothing risks pregnancy.

questions.q: Per 1,000 condom users (13% typical failure), pregnancies/year:
questions.why: 13% of 1,000 = 0.13 × 1,000 = 130 pregnancies per year.

questions.q: Unprotected sex Wed 8 am: copper IUD EC window ends…
questions.why: A copper IUD works as EC up to 5 days after unprotected sex. Wednesday 8 am + 5 days = Monday 8 am.

options: EC delays ovulation and is not an abortion pill
questions.why: EC delays ovulation, and it does not end an established pregnancy. It does not prevent HIV and is not for daily use.

questions.q: Why should two condoms not be used together?
questions.why: Two condoms together create friction that raises the risk of tearing. It does not double protection, so use just one correctly.

questions.q: Compare typical-use failure: pill 7%, injectable 4%, copper IUD 0.8%. Which ordering is correct (most → least effective)?
questions.why: Lower typical failure means more effective: copper IUD 0.8% < injectable 4% < pill 7%. So the order is IUD > injectable > pill.

questions.q: Case: A man refuses vasectomy fearing weakness. Best evidence-based reply?
options: Vasectomy doesn't affect strength or erections; it's simpler than tubectomy
questions.why: Vasectomy does not affect strength, erections or sexual drive, and it is a simpler, safer procedure than female tubectomy. The fear of weakness is a myth.

questions.q: Why may fertility return later after DMPA injections than after pills?
options: The injected hormone takes months to clear
questions.why: After a DMPA injection the hormone stays in the body for months, so ovulation may return later than after stopping pills. It is still reversible and does not damage the ovaries.

courses.title: Unit 3 · STIs & HIV: prevention, testing, treatment & stigma
courses.summary: Common sexually transmitted infections (bacterial, viral, parasitic), symptoms and silent infections, prevention including condoms and the HPV and hepatitis B vaccines, HIV transmission, testing and free treatment in India, PEP and PrEP, U=U, and fighting stigma.
outcomes: Learners can classify common STIs and their treatability
Learners can explain prevention methods including vaccines
Learners can describe how HIV is and isn't transmitted
Learners can explain testing, ART, PEP, PrEP and U=U
Learners can respond to stigma with facts
courses.guardianNote: Factual, non-explicit information on sexually transmitted infections, HIV, prevention (condoms, vaccines, PEP/PrEP), testing and treatment in India, and reducing stigma. For health knowledge; reminds learners of the age of consent (18).

lessons.title: What STIs are — and why many are silent

scenes.text: At a college health talk, a doctor asks how many think STIs always cause symptoms. Most hands go up.
She explains many infections, like chlamydia, often cause no symptoms but can still harm fertility.
'That's why testing matters,' she says.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Bacterial (curable with antibiotics)**: chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis.
- **Parasitic (curable)**: trichomoniasis.
- **Viral (treatable/manageable, some preventable by vaccine)**: HIV, herpes (HSV), HPV, hepatitis B.
Spread mainly through sexual contact; some also through blood (HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis) and from mother to baby.

steps.title: Silent infections
steps.body: Many STIs have **no symptoms**, especially early. Possible signs: unusual discharge, burning when urinating, sores, ulcers or warts in the genital area, lower abdominal pain, pain during sex. Untreated infections can cause **pelvic inflammatory disease**, **infertility**, complications in pregnancy, and raise HIV risk.

steps.title: Solved example: classify
steps.body: Syphilis → bacterial, curable. HPV → viral, vaccine-preventable; some types cause cervical and other cancers. Herpes → viral, manageable, not cured. Trichomoniasis → parasitic, curable. Hepatitis B → viral, vaccine-preventable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'I'd know if I had one' — often not.
- 'You can tell by looking at someone' — no.
- Self-treating with chemist antibiotics — wrong drug/dose leads to resistance; get tested and treated properly, along with partners.

quiz.why: Many STIs have no symptoms, so a person can have and pass on an infection without knowing. That is why testing matters.
Chlamydia is a bacterial infection, so antibiotics cure it. It is not viral or fungal.
Untreated STIs can cause serious complications such as infertility, chronic pain and increased HIV risk. They do not improve health or immunity.
HPV (human papillomavirus) is a virus, and a vaccine can prevent infection with the types that cause most cervical cancers.
No, you can't tell an STI by looking, since many have no visible signs. Only testing can show it.

scenes.text: Class 9 girls in Riya's school are offered the HPV vaccine at a health drive.
Her mother asks: 'Why so young?'
The doctor explains it works best before any exposure to the virus, protecting against cervical cancer later.

steps.title: Prevention toolkit
steps.body:
- **Delaying sex / abstinence** and fewer partners lower risk.
- **Condoms** every time, correctly.
- **Vaccines**: **HPV** (recommended for girls around 9–14; many countries also vaccinate boys) and **hepatitis B** (part of India's routine immunisation).
- **Regular testing** for sexually active people, and partner treatment.
- **Not sharing needles, razors** or anything with blood.
- **Prenatal testing** to prevent mother-to-child transmission.

steps.title: Solved example: why vaccinate early?
steps.body: HPV vaccine prevents infection; it doesn't cure an existing one. Giving it at 9–14, before exposure, gives the best protection and needs fewer doses. **Cervical cancer** is one of the commonest cancers in Indian women and is largely preventable with vaccination plus screening.

steps.title: Testing in India
steps.body: Free/low-cost testing at government **ICTCs** (Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres), **STI/RTI clinics ('Suraksha clinics')** in district hospitals, and private labs. Results are confidential. NACO helpline **1097**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the pill or Copper-T prevents STIs.
- Skipping partner treatment → reinfection ('ping-pong').
- Using antiseptic washes as 'prevention' — they don't work.

items: I know condoms prevent most STIs and pregnancy
I know the HPV vaccine is best before exposure
I know hepatitis B is in routine immunisation
I know where an ICTC or Suraksha clinic is
I know the NACO helpline is 1097
I know partners must be treated too

quiz.why: The HPV vaccine works best before exposure, around ages 9–14. It prevents infection rather than treating one that has occurred.
ICTC stands for Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre, where free HIV counselling and testing is available.
The NACO national AIDS helpline number is 1097. 181 is the Women's Helpline and 1098 is Childline.
No, the pill prevents pregnancy but gives no protection against STIs, including HIV. Only barriers like condoms reduce STI risk.
Treating partners too prevents reinfection; otherwise an untreated partner can pass the infection back ('ping-pong'). It doesn't prevent pregnancy.

lessons.title: HIV: transmission, myths and what does NOT spread it

scenes.text: A rumour spreads that a classmate's father has HIV. Some children refuse to share the lunch table.
The teacher calmly explains how HIV is and isn't transmitted.
The next day, the class eats together as usual.

steps.title: What HIV is
steps.body: **HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)** attacks CD4 immune cells. Without treatment it can progress to **AIDS** (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) over years. With treatment, people live long, healthy lives.

steps.title: How HIV spreads
steps.body: Through specific body fluids — **blood, semen, pre-seminal fluid, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, breast milk** — via: unprotected sex, sharing needles/syringes, unscreened blood transfusion, and from mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding (largely preventable with treatment).

steps.title: How HIV does NOT spread
steps.body: Hugging, shaking hands, sharing food, utensils, toilets, swimming pools, classrooms, mosquito bites, coughing, sneezing, tears, sweat or saliva in normal contact. **Discrimination against people living with HIV is prohibited** under the **HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act 2017** — including in schools and workplaces.

steps.title: Solved example: risk or no risk?
steps.body:
(a) Sharing a tiffin → **no risk**.
(b) Sharing a needle → **risk**.
(c) Mosquito bite → **no risk** (HIV doesn't replicate in mosquitoes).
(d) Unprotected sex with a partner of unknown status → **risk**; testing and condoms reduce it.
(e) Getting a tattoo with an unsterile needle → **risk**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Avoiding people living with HIV — that's stigma, and illegal discrimination.
- 'Only certain groups get HIV' — anyone can.

statements.s: HIV can spread by sharing food or utensils.
Mosquitoes can transmit HIV.
Sharing needles can transmit HIV.
Discrimination against people with HIV is prohibited in India by a 2017 Act.
With treatment, people with HIV can live long lives.

quiz.why: HIV attacks CD4 immune (T-helper) cells, weakening the immune system. It does not target bones, neurons or red cells.
HIV spreads through blood, so sharing needles can transmit it. Hugging, coughing and sharing a toilet don't spread it.
No, mosquito bites do not spread HIV, since the virus doesn't survive or multiply in mosquitoes.
India's HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act was passed in 2017, protecting people from discrimination.
Mother-to-child transmission of HIV is largely preventable with treatment during pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding (PMTCT). It is not certain or unpreventable.

lessons.title: HIV testing, ART, PEP, PrEP and U=U

scenes.text: Arun, 28, was diagnosed with HIV three years ago.
He takes one ART pill daily from a government ART centre for free.
His viral load is undetectable. 'I work, play cricket, plan a family. HIV is part of my life, not all of it.'

steps.title: Testing
steps.body: Rapid tests and lab tests at ICTCs and hospitals; results confidential; counselling before and after. There's a **window period** (weeks to ~3 months depending on the test) when a recent infection may not show — retest if advised.

steps.title: ART (antiretroviral therapy)
steps.body: Daily medicines that keep HIV under control. India provides **free ART** at government ART centres under NACO. Starting early and taking it daily keeps the immune system healthy.

steps.title: U=U, PEP and PrEP
steps.body:
- **U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable)**: a person with HIV on effective treatment with a sustained **undetectable viral load** does **not** transmit HIV sexually.
- **PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis)**: 28 days of medicines started **within 72 hours** (sooner is better) after a possible exposure (e.g. needle-stick, sexual assault). Go to a hospital immediately.
- **PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis)**: medicine taken before exposure by people at higher risk, under medical supervision.

steps.title: Solved example: PEP timing
steps.body: Possible exposure Saturday 9 pm → PEP must start before **Tuesday 9 pm** (72 h), ideally within hours. Sunday morning visit to the emergency department is far better than Tuesday evening.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing too early after exposure and assuming a negative is final.
- Stopping ART when feeling well.
- Thinking PEP is a 'morning-after pill' to use regularly.

activity.prompt: Within how many hours after a possible HIV exposure must PEP be started?

options: undetectable viral load = no sexual transmission
quiz.why: U=U means Undetectable = Untransmittable: a person on ART with an undetectable viral load does not sexually transmit HIV. It does not mean the virus is gone, so ART must continue.
PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) must start within 72 hours of exposure, and the sooner the better. After that it is less likely to work.

quiz.q: ART in India at government centres is…
quiz.why: ART is provided free at government ART centres in India, so cost should not stop treatment.

options: recent infection may not show on a test yet
quiz.why: The window period is the time after infection when a test may not yet detect it. So a recent exposure can give a false negative, and retesting is needed.
PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) is taken before exposure by people at risk, under medical supervision. It isn't for children or after a year.

questions.why: Chlamydia is caused by bacteria, so antibiotics treat it. It is not fungal, viral or genetic.
The NACO national AIDS helpline is 1097. 1930 is for cyber fraud, 1098 is Childline and 181 is the Women's Helpline.
HIV does not spread by sharing food. It passes through blood, sexual fluids and from mother to child, not through casual contact.
The HPV vaccine protects against the types of HPV that cause most cervical cancers. It does not prevent dengue, TB or asthma.
ART (antiretroviral therapy) is daily medication for HIV that keeps the viral load low. It is not a test, vaccine or antibiotic.
Many STIs are silent, with no symptoms, so a person may not know. That is why regular testing matters.

questions.q: Assertion: Partners should be treated together. Reason: Otherwise reinfection can occur.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. If only one partner is treated, the other can pass the infection back, so both should be treated together.
Mosquito bites do not transmit HIV, because the virus does not survive or multiply in mosquitoes. HIV spreads through unscreened blood, shared needles and from mother to baby without treatment.

questions.q: Testing centre in Indian public hospitals:
questions.why: ICTC (Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre) in public hospitals offers free, confidential HIV testing and counselling.

questions.q: Case: A student is excluded from class because her mother has HIV. This is…
questions.why: Excluding a child from class because a parent has HIV is illegal discrimination under the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017. HIV doesn't spread through classroom contact.

questions.q: Exposure Monday 6 am. Latest PEP start:
questions.why: PEP must start within 72 hours of exposure. Monday 6 am + 72 h (3 days) = Thursday 6 am.

options: They're at highest cancer risk now
questions.why: The HPV vaccine works best when given before exposure to the virus, so it targets ages 9–14. It prevents infection and does not cure it.

options: Sustained undetectable viral load prevents sexual transmission
questions.why: U=U: a sustained undetectable viral load on ART means HIV is not passed on sexually. It isn't a cure, so ART must continue.

questions.q: Case: Someone tests negative 1 week after a risk. What next?
options: Retest after the window period as advised
questions.why: A test one week after a risk may be negative because of the window period, so retest after the window period as advised. A single early negative can't be trusted.

questions.q: Which STI group is curable with medicine?
questions.why: Chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis are bacterial or parasitic, so medicines can cure them. HIV, herpes, HPV and hepatitis B are viral and can be managed or prevented, but are not simply cured.

questions.q: Why is self-treating with chemist antibiotics a problem?
options: Wrong drug/dose, untreated partners and resistance
questions.why: Self-treating with chemist antibiotics can mean the wrong drug or dose, leaves partners untreated and promotes antibiotic resistance. See a qualified doctor.

options: Condoms + vaccines (HPV, Hep B) + testing + partner treatment
questions.why: Best protection combines condoms, vaccines (HPV, Hep B), regular testing and partner treatment. Pills and Copper-T prevent pregnancy but not STIs, and antiseptic washes don't protect.

lessons.title: Is it pregnancy? Signs and tests

scenes.text: Married at 26, Nandini's period is 10 days late.
She buys a home pregnancy test; it shows two lines.
She visits the PHC to confirm and start antenatal care.

steps.title: Early signs
steps.body: Missed period · breast tenderness · nausea ('morning sickness', any time of day) · tiredness · passing urine more often · mood changes. Many of these can also have other causes; a **test** confirms.

steps.title: How tests work
steps.body: Home urine tests detect **hCG**, made after implantation. Most are reliable from the **first day of a missed period**; testing too early can give a false negative. A blood test can detect hCG earlier. Read instructions; morning urine is more concentrated.

steps.title: Solved example: when to test
steps.body: Cycle 30 days; last period began 1 March → next expected 31 March. Test from **31 March** onward; if negative but still no period after a week → retest or see a doctor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing the day after unprotected sex (too early).
- Assuming nausea = pregnancy.
- Ignoring severe abdominal pain with a positive test → may be **ectopic pregnancy** (outside the uterus) — **emergency**.

statements.s: Home pregnancy tests detect hCG.
A test the day after unprotected sex is reliable.
Severe one-sided abdominal pain with a positive test can be an emergency.
Morning sickness only happens in the morning.

quiz.why: Pregnancy tests detect hCG, a hormone made by the embryo's cells after implantation. LH, FSH and insulin are not the test marker.
Home tests are reliable from the first day of a missed period, when hCG is high enough to detect. Earlier tests may give a false negative.
An ectopic pregnancy grows outside the uterus, usually in a fallopian tube, and can cause dangerous internal bleeding. It is an emergency.

quiz.q: Next period due 15 May; test from…
quiz.why: Test from the first day of the missed period, so on the due date of 15 May. Testing earlier can miss low hCG levels.
Morning sickness is a misnomer, since nausea can happen at any time of day or night in pregnancy.

lessons.title: Antenatal care and teen pregnancy support

scenes.text: At her first antenatal visit, Lata gets a Mother and Child Protection card.
She's given iron–folic acid and calcium, tests, and a schedule of visits.
The nurse also explains danger signs and free transport for delivery.

steps.title: Antenatal care (India)
steps.body: Early registration; at least **4 antenatal visits** (WHO now recommends 8 contacts); blood pressure, weight, blood and urine tests, ultrasound; **iron–folic acid** and **calcium**; tetanus–diphtheria vaccine; nutrition counselling; **institutional delivery**. Government schemes support free care, delivery and transport (e.g. **Janani Suraksha Yojana**, **JSSK**; **PMMVY** cash benefit; **PMSMA** free check-ups on the 9th of each month).

steps.title: Danger signs — go to hospital
steps.body: Bleeding · severe headache or blurred vision · fits · high fever · severe abdominal pain · swelling of face/hands · reduced baby movements · water breaking early.

steps.title: Teen pregnancy
steps.body: Pregnancy under 18 has higher risks (anaemia, high BP, premature birth) and can disrupt education. A pregnant teen deserves **non-judgmental medical care and support**. For under-18s, POCSO requires reporting of sexual offences, and health providers will guide the process; confidential help: **1098**, adolescent-friendly health clinics (RKSK).

steps.title: Solved example: iron need
steps.body: If one IFA tablet daily is advised for 180 days from the second trimester, how many tablets? **180**. Taking them with vitamin C foods and not with tea helps absorption.

items: Take iron–folic acid and calcium as advised

quiz.why: Iron–folic acid tablets prevent anaemia and folic acid also lowers the risk of neural tube birth defects. They do not prevent diabetes, asthma or STIs.
Bleeding in pregnancy is a danger sign needing urgent medical care. Food cravings, mild tiredness and backache after work are common.
PMSMA (Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan) gives free antenatal check-ups on the 9th of every month at government facilities.
Teen pregnancy carries higher risks, including anaemia and premature birth, because the body is still growing. It does not give better health.
Childline 1098 offers free, confidential help for children under 18. 100 is police, 1930 is cybercrime and 14446 is not a children's helpline.

lessons.title: Safe abortion: the MTP Act (as amended 2021)

scenes.text: A college law-club session discusses reproductive rights in India.
They read the MTP Act's key provisions.
'So safe, legal abortion exists — but it must be by registered providers and within the rules.'

steps.title: Key provisions (topic level)
steps.body:
Under the **Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act 1971, as amended in 2021**:
- Up to **20 weeks**: on the opinion of **one** registered medical practitioner (RMP).
- **20–24 weeks**: opinion of **two** RMPs, for specified categories (e.g. survivors of sexual assault, minors, change in marital status, women with disabilities, foetal malformation risk, humanitarian settings).
- Beyond 24 weeks: for **substantial foetal abnormalities**, as decided by a state **Medical Board**.
- Grounds include risk to the woman's life or physical/mental health, and **contraceptive failure** (applies to any woman or her partner — not only married women).
- **Confidentiality** of the woman is protected.
- A minor or a mentally ill person needs a guardian's written consent.
- In 2022 the Supreme Court held that unmarried women have the same entitlement as married women under the Act.

steps.title: Safe vs unsafe
steps.body: Safe abortion is done by trained providers at approved facilities using recommended methods (medicines in early pregnancy under medical supervision, or procedures). **Unsafe abortion** (untrained people, unapproved pills without supervision) is a major cause of maternal deaths worldwide. Sex-selective abortion is **illegal** (PCPNDT Act).

steps.title: Solved example: which rule applies?
steps.body:
(a) 9 weeks, contraceptive failure → up to 20 weeks, one RMP.
(b) 22 weeks, minor survivor of assault → 20–24 weeks category, two RMPs (and POCSO reporting).
(c) 26 weeks, severe foetal abnormality → Medical Board.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not legal or medical advice. Consult a registered doctor at an approved facility.

activity.prompt: Match the gestation to the MTP rule
pairs: Opinion of one registered medical practitioner

quiz.why: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act of 1971 was amended in 2021, widening access and gestational limits.
Under the MTP Act, up to 20 weeks one registered medical practitioner (RMP) can approve termination. A Medical Board is needed only for later cases with foetal abnormalities.
After the 2021 amendment, the contraceptive-failure ground applies to any woman or her partner, not just married women.
Sex-selective abortion is illegal in India under the PCPNDT Act. It is not a choice or something to encourage.

quiz.q: Unsafe abortion is a major cause of…
quiz.why: Unsafe abortion causes bleeding, infection and organ damage, and it is a major cause of maternal deaths. Safe, legal services reduce this risk.

scenes.text: Rahul and Sneha, both 31, have been trying to conceive for two years.
Tests show low sperm count in Rahul and irregular ovulation in Sneha.
With treatment and counselling, they explore options together. 'It's nobody's fault — it's a medical issue.'

steps.title: What infertility is
steps.body: Not getting pregnant after **12 months** of regular unprotected sex (6 months if the woman is over 35). It affects roughly **1 in 6 people** worldwide (WHO). Causes are found in men, women, both, or are unexplained — so **both partners** should be evaluated.

steps.title: Common causes
steps.body: **Women**: ovulation problems (e.g. PCOS, thyroid), blocked tubes (often after infections), endometriosis, age. **Men**: low sperm count or motility, blockages, hormonal issues, varicocele. **Both**: smoking, alcohol, obesity or very low weight, some infections (untreated STIs), stress.

steps.title: Assisted reproductive technology (ART)
steps.body:
- **IUI** (intrauterine insemination): prepared sperm placed in the uterus.
- **IVF** (in-vitro fertilisation): eggs fertilised in a lab; embryos transferred to the uterus.
- **ICSI**: a single sperm injected into an egg.
In India, ART clinics and banks are regulated by the **ART (Regulation) Act 2021**; surrogacy by the **Surrogacy (Regulation) Act 2021**.

steps.title: Solved example: blame myth
steps.body:
Q: Is infertility 'the woman's problem'?
- Step 1: Male factors contribute in a large share of couples.
- Step 2: Both partners need tests (semen analysis is simple).
- **Conclusion:** myth; it's a shared medical concern.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Blaming women.
- Delaying evaluation for years.
- Unregulated 'miracle' fertility cures.

activity.prompt: Which partner can this cause affect?

quiz.why: Infertility is defined as not conceiving after 12 months of regular unprotected sex, for women under 35. One month or a week is too short.
WHO estimates about 1 in 6 people worldwide experience infertility in their lifetime. So it is common, not rare.
IVF is in vitro fertilisation, in which eggs are fertilised by sperm in a lab and the embryo is then placed in the uterus. It isn't a vaccine or herbal treatment.
Both partners should be tested, because male and female factors each cause infertility. Testing only one can miss the cause.

quiz.q: ART clinics in India are regulated by…
quiz.why: Assisted reproductive technology clinics in India are regulated by the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021. RTI, COTPA and POSH deal with other matters.

scenes.text: Since 16, Fatima has had periods so painful she faints.
At 24 a gynaecologist diagnoses endometriosis after years of being told 'it's normal'.
'Severe pain that stops your life is not normal — get it checked.'

steps.title: PCOS
steps.body: **Polycystic ovary syndrome**: common hormonal condition — irregular or absent periods, signs of higher androgens (acne, excess facial/body hair, scalp hair thinning), often polycystic-looking ovaries on ultrasound; linked to insulin resistance. Managed with lifestyle (activity, balanced diet), and medicines for symptoms or fertility. Long-term: check blood sugar, cholesterol.

steps.title: Endometriosis
steps.body: Tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus → severe period pain, pain during sex, heavy periods, fertility problems. Diagnosis is often delayed for years. Treatments: pain relief, hormonal therapy, surgery.

steps.title: Menopause
steps.body: Periods stop permanently, usually around **45–55** (often ~50 in India, sometimes earlier). Diagnosed after **12 months** without a period. Symptoms: hot flushes, sleep problems, mood changes, vaginal dryness, bone loss risk. Help: lifestyle, calcium/vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, and treatments discussed with a doctor. Men have gradual hormone changes with age too.

steps.title: Solved example: when to see a doctor
steps.body:
(a) Periods every 60–90 days with acne and chin hair at 19 → **PCOS check**.
(b) Period pain that makes you faint or miss school monthly → **check for endometriosis**.
(c) Bleeding after menopause → **see a doctor promptly**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Pain is part of being a woman' — severe pain deserves evaluation.
- 'PCOS means you can never have children' — many with PCOS conceive, sometimes with treatment.

activity.prompt: Match the condition to its feature
pairs: Lining-like tissue outside the uterus; severe pain

quiz.why: PCOS is closely linked to insulin resistance, which raises male-type hormones and disturbs ovulation. It is not mainly a bone, eye or vitamin problem.
Endometriosis, where womb-lining tissue grows outside the uterus, typically causes severe period pain. It is not just fever and isn't always symptom-free.
Menopause is confirmed after 12 consecutive months without a period. A shorter gap could be an irregular cycle.
No. PCOS does not always mean infertility, because many women with PCOS conceive, sometimes with treatment.
Any bleeding after menopause is abnormal and a red flag, so see a doctor. It can sometimes signal a serious condition and shouldn't be ignored.

questions.why: Pregnancy tests detect hCG, made by the embryo's cells after implantation. LH, FSH and oxytocin are not the test marker.
The MTP Act was amended in 2021, widening eligibility and gestational limits.
WHO estimates infertility affects about 1 in 6 people. It is common, not rare.
IFA (iron–folic acid) tablets prevent anaemia in pregnancy. They don't prevent HIV, diabetes or STIs.
Up to 20 weeks, one registered medical practitioner (RMP) can approve an MTP under the amended Act. A Medical Board or court is not needed.
Menopause usually occurs between about 45 and 55 years, when ovarian hormone production falls.

questions.q: Assertion: Both partners should be evaluated for infertility. Reason: Male factors are common causes.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Male factors are common causes, so both partners should be evaluated.

questions.q: Severe one-sided pain with a positive test may mean…
questions.why: Severe one-sided pain with a positive pregnancy test suggests an ectopic pregnancy, a medical emergency. It is not normal, twins or PCOS.
The PCPNDT Act bans prenatal sex determination, to stop sex-selective abortion. It does not ban IVF, contraception or all ultrasound.

questions.q: Case: 19-year-old with 70-day cycles, acne, chin hair. Likely check for…
questions.why: Cycles of 70 days with acne and chin hair point to PCOS, a hormone condition, and the person should be checked by a doctor. Pregnancy should also be excluded, but PCOS is the likely cause.

questions.q: 22 weeks, minor survivor of assault: MTP rule?
questions.why: Between 20 and 24 weeks, MTP is allowed for special categories such as survivors of assault (including minors), with two RMPs' opinion. One RMP is only for up to 20 weeks.

questions.q: Next period due 10 June; earliest reliable home test:
questions.why: Test from the first day of the missed period, which here is 10 June. Earlier, hCG may be too low to detect.

questions.q: Which is a correct statement about ICSI?
options: A single sperm is injected into an egg
questions.why: ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection) is an IVF technique where a single sperm is injected directly into an egg. It isn't sperm placed in the uterus, tubal surgery or a vaccine.
Endometriosis is often diagnosed late, delayed for years, because pain is wrongly dismissed as normal period pain. It is not diagnosed with a pregnancy test.

questions.q: Case: A woman with contraceptive failure, unmarried, 10 weeks pregnant. Under the amended Act?
options: Eligible — contraceptive-failure ground applies to any woman; one RMP up to 20 weeks
questions.why: After the 2021 amendment, the contraceptive-failure ground applies to any woman, married or not, and one RMP can approve up to 20 weeks. So at 10 weeks she is eligible.

options: Untrained providers/unsupervised methods cause bleeding, infection, death
questions.why: Unsafe abortion by untrained people or unsupervised methods can cause heavy bleeding, infection and death. Safe abortion should be done by qualified providers.

questions.q: Which statement about infertility is MOST accurate?
options: Causes may be female, male, both or unexplained; both should be tested
questions.why: Infertility can have female, male, combined or unexplained causes, so both partners should be tested. It isn't always the woman, genetic or due to stress.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Adult sexual & reproductive health: check-ups, screening & common concerns
courses.summary: Clinical, non-explicit adult health literacy: routine sexual-health check-ups and STI testing, cervical, breast and testicular awareness and screening, common concerns (erectile difficulties, low desire, pain during sex, premature ejaculation) as medical topics, pornography myths vs reality, and how to find trustworthy care.
outcomes: Learners can plan routine sexual and reproductive health check-ups
Learners can describe cervical screening and breast and testicular awareness
Learners can describe common sexual-function concerns as treatable health issues
Learners can separate pornography myths from reality
Learners can choose qualified, trustworthy care and avoid quackery

lessons.title: Routine check-ups, STI testing and screening

scenes.text: At 30, Priya books her first cervical screening and a general check-up.
The doctor explains a quick test, the HPV vaccine, and breast self-awareness.
'Prevention is easier than cure,' she tells her friends — who book too.

steps.title: Cervical screening
steps.body: Detects pre-cancer changes before cancer develops. India's national screening uses **VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid)** for women **30–65** at government facilities; **HPV DNA tests** and **Pap smears** are also used (commonly every 3–5 years depending on test). The **HPV vaccine** plus screening can prevent most cervical cancer.

steps.title: Breast & testicular awareness
steps.body: **Breast**: know what's normal for you; report a new lump, skin dimpling, nipple changes or discharge, or persistent pain; **clinical breast examination** is offered in national screening programmes; mammography per doctor's advice, commonly from about 40–50. **Testicles**: report a new hard lump, swelling, heaviness — testicular cancer peaks at 15–35 and is highly curable early.

steps.title: STI testing
steps.body: Sexually active adults — especially with new or multiple partners — benefit from periodic testing for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C, and others as advised. ICTCs and Suraksha clinics provide confidential tests; private labs too.

steps.title: Solved example: a screening plan
steps.body:
Woman, 32: VIA/HPV test now; repeat per result (e.g. 5 years); monthly breast awareness; BP, sugar, thyroid as advised.
Man, 28: testicular awareness; STI tests if new partner; BP and sugar checks.
Both: vaccines (hepatitis B if not immune; HPV catch-up as per doctor).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping screening because there are 'no symptoms' — that's exactly when it works.
- Feeling embarrassed — clinicians do this every day.

items: STI testing when there's a new partner
Hepatitis B and HPV vaccine status checked

quiz.q: India's national cervical screening (VIA) age range:
quiz.why: India's national programme screens women aged 30–65 for cervical cancer using VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid). It is not for 10–20 or only 18–25.
Testicular cancer is most common in young men aged about 15–35. It is rare in young children and older men.

options: a new lump or nipple changes
quiz.why: A new breast lump or nipple changes should be reported to a doctor. Normal monthly tenderness, tan and freckles are not warning signs.
Screening works best before symptoms appear, so problems are found early when they are easier to treat. Waiting until you are ill or have cancer defeats its purpose.
Confidential STI testing is available at ICTC and Suraksha clinics. Banks, post offices and schools don't provide it.

lessons.title: Common sexual-function concerns as health issues

scenes.text: Vikram, 35, has had erection difficulties for months and is too embarrassed to talk.
His GP checks BP, sugar and cholesterol — and finds early diabetes.
'Your body was sending a signal. Treating diabetes and stress will help.'

steps.title: Common concerns (clinical overview)
steps.body:
- **Erectile difficulties**: common with age, stress, diabetes, high BP, smoking, alcohol, some medicines; can be an **early sign of heart disease or diabetes**.
- **Premature ejaculation**: common; behavioural techniques, counselling and medicines help.
- **Low desire**: affected by stress, depression, relationship issues, hormones, medicines.
- **Pain during sex** (for any gender): infections, dryness (e.g. after childbirth or menopause), endometriosis, vaginismus — treatable.
These are **medical/psychological topics**, not personal failures.

steps.title: Who to see
steps.body: Family doctor, gynaecologist, urologist/andrologist, psychiatrist or qualified **sexual-medicine specialist** or counsellor. Avoid roadside 'sex clinics', unregulated 'herbal' boosters (some contain hidden drugs) and online pills without prescription.

steps.title: Solved example: think like a clinician
steps.body:
Concern: erection difficulty, age 45, smoker, BP 150/95.
- Step 1: Check cardiovascular risk (BP, sugar, lipids).
- Step 2: Lifestyle: stop smoking, exercise, sleep, limit alcohol.
- Step 3: Review medicines; address stress or relationship factors.
- Step 4: Treatment options with a doctor.

steps.title: Myths
steps.body:
- 'Semen loss causes weakness' (dhat myth) — no evidence.
- 'Size determines satisfaction' — communication and relationship matter far more.
- 'Masturbation causes impotence' — no.

statements.s: Erectile difficulties can be an early sign of heart disease or diabetes.
Roadside 'sex clinics' are a reliable source of care.
Pain during sex is usually treatable.
Masturbation causes impotence.

quiz.why: Erection problems can signal underlying vascular (blood vessel) disease or diabetes, so a check-up is worthwhile. They are not a sign of vitamin excess or asthma.
Get help from a qualified doctor, urologist or sexual-medicine specialist. Roadside clinics, herbal boosters and online pills without prescription are risky.
Low sexual desire can be linked to stress, depression and certain medicines. It has nothing to do with eye colour, shoe size or height.
Unregulated boosters can contain hidden drugs, which can be dangerous. They are not just vitamins or herbs.
Dhat syndrome, the belief that semen loss causes weakness, is a myth. Semen loss does not cause illness, though the anxiety it causes is real and can be treated.

scenes.text: Arjun, 22, feels anxious that real life doesn't match what he's seen online.
A counsellor explains how pornography is staged, edited and often shows non-consensual or unrealistic behaviour.
He learns real intimacy is about communication, consent and respect.

steps.title: What pornography is (and isn't)
steps.body: Commercial pornography is **performance**: scripted, edited, with performers chosen for appearance, often without showing consent, protection or communication. It is not sex education. Heavy use can shape unrealistic expectations about bodies, performance and consent, and for some people becomes compulsive.

steps.title: Law (topic level)
steps.body: In India, viewing/possessing/sharing **child sexual abuse material** is a serious crime (POCSO, IT Act 67B). Publishing or transmitting obscene or sexually explicit material is regulated under IT Act 67/67A. Sharing intimate images without consent is a crime.

steps.title: Solved example: myth vs reality
steps.body:
Myth: bodies look like performers'. Reality: huge natural variation.
Myth: everyone wants the same things. Reality: preferences differ; **ask and listen**.
Myth: 'no' means 'convince me'. Reality: no means no; consent is ongoing.
Myth: protection isn't needed. Reality: condoms and testing matter.

steps.title: If use feels out of control
steps.body: Signs: using more than intended, failing to cut down, harm to relationships/work/sleep. Help: counselling (CBT), screen blockers, addressing loneliness or anxiety, **14416**.

items.text: Porn shows what normal bodies look like
Consent should be ongoing and clear
Performance in porn is scripted and edited

quiz.why: Commercial pornography is a staged performance made for entertainment, not reality, education or medical advice. It gives unrealistic ideas about bodies and sex.
Child sexual abuse material is a serious crime to view, possess or share in India. It is not private, art or legal.
Real intimacy depends on communication and consent. Copying videos, guessing or pressure damages trust.
Compulsive use can be helped by counselling, blocking software and support such as Tele-MANAS 14416. More use or secrecy tends to deepen the problem.
Sharing intimate images without consent is a crime, a privacy violation under Indian law. It is never a joke or normal.

scenes.text: Painted ads on a wall promise 'guaranteed cure for all secret diseases'.
Neha checks: no qualified doctor's name, no registration number.
She goes to the district hospital's Suraksha clinic instead.

steps.title: Signs of trustworthy care
steps.body: Qualified doctor with a registration number (State Medical Council/NMC); clear fees; privacy; explains options and side effects; doesn't promise 'guaranteed cures'; doesn't shame you.

steps.title: Trustworthy information
steps.body: Government health portals (MoHFW, NACO), WHO, national professional bodies, your doctor. Be wary of forums, influencers selling products, and 'miracle' herbal cures.

steps.title: Solved example: rate the source
steps.body: Wall ad 'guaranteed cure, secret disease' → ❌. District hospital Suraksha clinic → ✅. Influencer selling a 'stamina' powder → ❌. WHO fact sheet → ✅.

steps.title: General education
steps.body: This is general education, not medical advice. See a qualified doctor for personal concerns.

quiz.why: A 'guaranteed cure' claim is a red flag of quackery, because honest doctors can't guarantee results. Explaining side effects, showing a registration number and privacy are good signs.
Trustworthy health information comes from official sources like NACO, MoHFW and WHO. Wall ads, random forums and influencer sales pitches are unreliable.
Doctors are registered with the State Medical Council or NMC (National Medical Commission). Banks, schools or police don't register doctors.
Be wary of online pills sold without a prescription, as they may be fake, unsafe or contain hidden drugs.

questions.q: Cervical screening test in national programme:
questions.why: VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) is the cervical screening test used in the national programme. MRI, X-ray and ECG are not used for this.
Testicular cancer peaks in young men aged about 15–35, so awareness is useful at that age.
'Guaranteed cure' is a quack red flag, because no honest doctor can guarantee a cure. A registration number, privacy and explaining risks are good signs.
HPV vaccination plus screening prevents most cervical cancers, because HPV causes nearly all of them. It doesn't prevent fractures, heart attacks or colds.
Pornography is a staged performance, not reality, education or medical advice.
ICTC offers confidential HIV and STI counselling and testing. Libraries, banks and ATMs don't.

questions.q: Assertion: Erectile difficulties may warn of heart disease. Reason: Both can share blood-vessel causes.
questions.why: Both are true and R explains A. Erectile difficulty and heart disease can share blood-vessel causes, so one may warn of the other.
'Masturbation causes impotence' is a myth with no medical evidence. Condoms do prevent STIs, pain during sex can be treated and screening helps.
Skin dimpling or a new lump in the breast are red flags that need medical review. Stretch marks, freckles and monthly tenderness are normal.

questions.q: Case: A man buys 'herbal stamina' pills online. Concern?
options: Hidden drugs and no medical check
questions.why: Online 'herbal stamina' pills may contain hidden drugs and are taken without any medical check, which is risky. They are not always government-approved or just vitamins.

questions.q: Case: Woman, 34, never screened. Best advice?
options: Cervical screening now; breast awareness; follow-up per result
questions.why: A 34-year-old woman who has never been screened should have cervical screening now (the programme covers ages 30–65), keep breast awareness and follow up per result. Waiting for symptoms is not advised.

questions.q: Why see a doctor for erectile difficulty at 45 with high BP?
options: Check cardiovascular risk and treat causes
questions.why: At 45 with high BP, erectile difficulty may point to vascular disease, so a doctor can check cardiovascular risk and treat causes. Powders and ignoring it are unsafe.

questions.q: Which is TRUE about child sexual abuse material in India?
options: Viewing, possessing or sharing is a serious crime
questions.why: Viewing, possessing or sharing child sexual abuse material is a serious crime in India. It is not legal to view, and the law applies not only to sharing or abroad.
NACO and WHO are official, evidence-based sources. Forum rumours, wall ads and influencers may mislead or be selling something.

questions.q: Case: Compulsive porn use harming sleep and relationships. Best response?
questions.why: Compulsive use is best handled with counselling (such as CBT), blocking software, addressing underlying stress and help like 14416. More use, hiding it or ignoring it doesn't help.

questions.q: Which combination best protects reproductive health in adults?
options: Vaccines, screening, STI testing, qualified care
questions.why: Reproductive health is protected by vaccines, screening, STI testing and care from qualified doctors. Herbal boosters, online pills and avoiding doctors add risk.

options: Knowing what's normal helps spot changes early
questions.why: Knowing what is normal for your body helps you notice changes early and see a doctor sooner. It does not diagnose cancer or replace doctors.
